speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, March 11, 1983, consideration in Committee of Bill C-139, to amend the statute law relating to income tax (No. 2)-Mr. Lalonde-Mr. Corbin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. The Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Deniger) has the floor.
On Clause 1-Value of benefits

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take advantage of this opportunity, in the debate on the Income Tax Bill, to make a few comments on automobile standby charges. For many hours the House has been debating this Bill and particularly the policy on automobile standby charges. Like most Members, I have received a host of recommendations and advice regarding this new tax. Of course, the easy way out would be to remove the tax altogether. However, I do not think that would be wise, in view of the extent of the Government's deficit and its financial requirements.
I feel that as responsible legislators, we should not be considering the nature of this tax but its methodology and application. When I discuss the matter with my constituents who include some of those 140,000 Canadians who are driving cars or vehicles provided by their employers, they all agree, Mr. Chairman, that there is a certain time during which they drive the car or vehicles for personal use, and they fully understand that this is a benefit that constitutes income, and that like any income it should be taxed, and I think it is irresponsible to try and argue against this principle.
What I would like to suggest to the Minister-whether he does it in this Bill or in the next budget-is a new method for collecting this tax.
[DOT]	(1110)
At the present time, car users, car dealers and travelling salesmen are responsible for these charges, which means they
themselves must keep track of what is personal use and what is not. There is a proposal before the House to set the monthly standby charge at 2 per cent of the cost of a car belonging to the employer, and so forth.
I think that if I were to draft this legislation, I would do it quite differently. I would put the onus on the employer, and I shall explain. Instead of taxing the user, I would tax the company, which would be done as follows. A company that provides a car to an employee has thereby incurred an expense that is tax-deductible, and I would like the company to charge the employee, that is, the user, an amount for the personal value of this service. For instance, if the car has a four-cylinder engine, the employer could charge $40 a month, $60 for six cylinders and $80 for eight cylinders, for personal use by the employee. What does the employee have to do? The employee who, let us say, has a nice car, a V-8, for instance, would have to pay $80 a month, after paying taxes. This is what is called after-tax dollars, and the amount would be paid to the company, which would then be taxed on this additional income.
This way, the Government's main goal, to tax personal use, has been achieved, because we are taxing the employer. Instead of taxing 140,000 users, we would then be taxing perhaps 1,000 employers who are providing cars to these users. From the accounting point of view, it would seem to be a far simpler, more practical and more effective procedure. I also feel that the employee, who would have a monthly premium to pay, would realize what his car is worth daily and monthly. That is quite clear, and as far as the company is concerned, it would be very happy to use that method.
Mr. Chairman, this is not an original proposal, because as you probably know, the same method is being used in various States in the US. It is a foolproof method and a very satisfactory one as far as the Government's objectives are concerned. That being said-and I agree with the Government that personal use should be taxed since it is a benefit or income and as such should be taxed-it seems to me that we should ensure that not employees but employers are responsible for the tax on this benefit. While I am on the subject of cars, I shall, if I may, say a few words about capital cost allowance and how it affects the automobile industry.

March 15, 1983
Income Tax
Earlier, before the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Cosgrove) was asking for a borrowing authority of several billion dollars. The increase in the Government's borrowing requirements and the deficit is of course due to the fact that this year, the Government had to spend about $8 billion, if I am not mistaken, on additional unemployment insurance benefits. It seems the additional amount is needed as a result of the disastrous situation in the automobile industry, which is mainly concentrated in Central Canada-in Ontario and at Sainte-Therese. What should be understood when discussing the automobile industry is that the industry has a very broad impact in Canada. As a result, there are workers who have lost their jobs, in every riding in the country.
I feel that if we are to make a positive contribution towards helping the automobile industry, which is the largest employer in Canada, perhaps, in addition to reconsidering automobile standby charges as I mentioned earlier, we could also take another look at the rules for capital cost allowance for cars that are leased or purchased by companies.
Mr. Chairman, yesterday a delegation of dealers in Japanese cars met with the Minister of International Trade (Mr. Regan). They complained about the fact that the measures we have adopted have resulted in the loss of 2,300 jobs. I for one would prefer to use tax measures to help the automobile industry, and I think the best way to do that would be to increase the capital cost allowance on North American cars.
We used to have 30 per cent for the first year. Our budget has restricted this to 30 per cent for the first six months and 15 per cent for the last six months. However, the 15 per cent for the last six months constitutes a real danger to the automobile leasing industry and is in fact jeopardizing the very survival of Canadian car dealers. I realize that the Government urgently requires substantial amounts of money. In fact, I share its views on the aims of the Income Tax Act. However, I do have some problems with respect to the application of this legislation to the automobiles. Furthermore, I would like the Minister to consider the amendment we proposed a few months ago, by which a capital cost allowance of up to 40 per cent would be allowed companies such as Tilden, Hertz, Avis and others, on cars rented on the daily basis.
I wish the Government would consider this amendment for the benefit of thousands of car dealers and thousands of companies engaging in automobile leasing, for the benefit of hundreds of companies which buy fleets of cars which are of course of North American origin, often built in Canada. If they were not built in Detroit or Toledo, these cars are from Windsor or Oshawa or Sainte-Therese. These are cars that were built here. What is happening now is that the new tax system discourages companies from purchasing North American cars and is in fact an incentive to purchase imported cars which may be made in Japan or in Germany.
In concluding, Mr. Chairman, I would like the Minister to give some thought to the comments I have just made. I am
anxious to hear his reply. I would also like to make a few comments subsequent to the Minister's reply. However, if the Minister is unable to respond-and I am aware that it is important to complete consideration of this Bill as soon as possible so that taxpayers can receive their tax refunds-if the Minister is unable to give the House a satisfactory answer right away, I would like him to consider my comments as representations in connection with the budget we all hope will be brought down within the next few weeks.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the Hon. Member for his thoughtful presentation and his recommendations to myself and the Minister of Finance. There is no question that the Hon. Member put his observations in the context of total Government responsibility. For example, he indicated that any benefit offered to one segment of the community under our tax domain is quantifiable and no doubt can be equated to income. If there is no tax on such benefit, it means that other Canadians have to carry that charge through paying taxes in some other area. Therefore, I appreciate that the Hon. Member thought about that in his question.
The Hon. Member prefaced his question by saying that any feature of the tax system that gives a preference or permits a deduction or exemption is a charge on the over-all Government operation and finally becomes part of the deficit and the borrowing Bill which was before the Finance Committee.
Similarly, I am pleased that the Hon. Member has drawn our attention to the competition between the North American product and the imported product. He used the example of Japanese vehicles. There was one point he did not comment on either in his preface or his larger presentation. That is an alternate way of assisting the North American industry in selling its product and thereby either maintaining present employment levels or, optimistically, looking at prospects for potential growth of the North American industry.
With the greatest respect to the Hon. Member, I do not think the answer to the health of that industry is through Government action in giving exemptions, either by way of depreciation or waiving of income benefits that some people receive. In effect, the economy would then be carrying one sector that is not competing. The difficulty is that the sector is not competing.
The problem with the North American product is that other countries, including Japan and Europe, are offering products such as vehicles which the Canadian public wants to buy. They express their preference with their pocketbook. The only answer is for the industry to compete better. We cannot expect the Government to set the standards and be the final arbiter as to what products Canadians are going to purchase. One of the reasons the industry is not doing well is that Canadians in large numbers are buying other products. I think there is a message there for the industry.

Mr. Chairman, I look forward to the comments of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, as usual, but I would like to clear one important matter up.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, 1 would like to point out that the Hon. Member for La Prairie has consistently given us outstanding advice on these matters over the past year. I have filled my office as Parliamentary Secretary for almost a year now and throughout that period the Hon. Member has discussed with us the problems associated with the standby charges and with capital cost allowances. His advice has been vital in making up the final version of this Bill. I believe he would like us to go a little further and to be even more understanding, and 1 compliment him on his vigour and enthusiasm in raising these issues. We saw a good deal of his understanding of the matter in his discussion earlier.
He went right to the core of the question in saying that "personal use" is the key issue. He then suggested to us an interesting method whereby the employer would collect a rebate from an employee for personal use of an automobile.
I would point out to the Hon. Member that under Revenue Canada's interpretation bulletin IT-63R, we find under Section 6, and I quote:
A payment by an employee to his employer for his personal use of the automobile reduces the benefit added to income under paragraph 6(l)(a).
He will find if he goes to the existing Act and to this Bill that the same provision is carried on. It is a question of degree after that. He has pursued an opportunity which is already in the law. He is suggesting to us that for a simplification we should use this everywhere. I believe it is a very good idea, one that warrants the consideration of the Minister of Finance, and I will personally ensure that he takes a good look at it. I would also ask the Hon. Member to point out to employers and to his

Mr. Chairman, I believe we have had a rather long discussion with respect to Clause 1. I just wanted to make two or three points with respect to the amendment, and unless other Members really want to say more with respect to automobiles, I propose we move on to other sections of the Act.
As you know, sir, it has been our position that this Act should have full and complete discussion as far as possible. Frankly, we spent rather longer than I had hoped on Clause 1 on Friday, and it is unfortunate that the Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary refused to answer questions appropriately, particularly those of the Hon. Member for Calgary West. Had they done that, we would have moved out of Clause 1 earlier.
Speaking to the amendment, sir, at the top of page 2 Members will note Clause l(a)(iii) reads:
-that was a benefit in relation to the use of an automobile, except to the extent that it related to the operation of the automobile;

March 15, 1983
Income Tax
When you read that it does not make any sense at all, so you go to the explanatory notes which the Minister said were so clear and everyone could understand. We have asked the Minister to explain those explanatory notes but he cannot. The explanatory notes say that this amendment adds that Subclause to provide an exception for any benefit relating to the availability of an automobile for personal use, but clarifies that operating costs of an automobile used for personal purposes which are paid for by the employer must be included in income.
Well, Mr. Chairman, what we are saying is that the operating costs to be included in income should be restricted to the actual operating costs of the automobile, essentially the fuel. Remember, this is the employer's car and the employee is using it part-time for personal use. As to the licence, obviously the owner has to license the car and there is no reason why that charge should be borne in part by the employee. When you get to the question of insurance, in the case of a salesman's automobile it is usually much higher than that which the individual himself might pay, particularly in view of the fact that corporations often insure for much higher limits than individuals would necessarily insure themselves. Therefore, because of the wording of the Clause, the employee is being asked to pay a disproportionately high charge for maintenance.
This has never been the law in the past which is why this amendment is here. It is a further burden on the employee. You will recall, sir, that we objected to the inclusion of this particular part because it was not within the Ways and Means motion, but the Chair ruled it was. Nonetheless, this is a further burden on the employee. We say that burden should be restricted to the actual cost of operating the vehicle, the gasoline in the tank. If the employer pays the gas bill, then the employee should pick up his share of the gas bill with reference to his mileage.
If we could have a reply from the Minister on that, and perhaps some other views, I think we could get on with the Bill at this point.

Mr. Chairman, the Government does not support the amendment and we would be prepared to express our view in a vote very quickly. The difficulty in the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South is that we do not share with him whatever rationale he has for drawing the distinction between fuel and other expenses. For example, what is the rationale for exempting the cost of tires, grease or oil and not that of fuel? Similarly, the cost of insurance or a licence. The car will not go without fuel, and it certainly should not be on the road without insurance or a licence. We find no rationale for the amendment and cannot accept it for that reason.

Mr. Chairman, on the same subject I would like to read into the record a letter to the Minister of Finance, a copy of which I received. I will not read the whole thing, but I
would like some clarification on it for my constituents. The constituent writes:
It grieves me considerably to have to write to you on a situation you have inherited with your position. However, my grievance is costing me considerably, all a result of the increased tax portion of my company automobile.
It is costing me $3,158.16 taxable benefits portion annually, for an automobile worth $10,049.48 annually (all costs included). That represents 31 per cent. My personal mileage, 10,000 km versus 45,600 km business mileage represents only 21.9 per cent "Real Value" or to rephrase the statement I'm taxed 1/3 on 1/5 value, net.
He then goes on to talk about some other personal problems and ends with this paragraph:
With these excessive tax rates and nasty twists being annually developed, how is one expected to get ahead? Why is the incentive to perform and exceed being taken away, especially from the young who will one day be expected to take over the management and operation of our businesses, provinces and country.
Now, I would like to inquire of the Minister or his Parliamentary Secretary what kind of answer I should give my constituent. Whether or not you want to include tires, gasoline or insurance, or whatever, what do I say to him about the proportion of personal use involved, roughly one-fifth, and is there any chance that there could be a proportionate write-off in some way to assist him?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the Hon. Member's representation. I think there are many taxpayers with similar specific questions so I am sure that more than just that one person will find this question useful. I hope I will be able to answer to his satisfaction.
We have set the 12,000 kilometre minimum standby charge because we believe that is roughly what everyone else would pay for personal use of the car. We have used 12,000 kilometres as a reasonable cut-off point. Many people will use business cars for smaller portions of personal use, but by the time you get to 12,000 kilometres you are using your car for roughly the same amount of personal use as most other citizens would be. So the Government has, perhaps arbitrarily, drawn a line and said that at 12,000 kilometres everyone is being treated equally. It is what everybody would drive personally and it is also what other people would pay in after tax charges.
However, I ask the Hon. Member to remember two or three qualifiers. First of all, it is the personal choice of the taxpayer to drive the company car for personal use. The taxpayer can easily decide not to do so, to use either other methods of transportation or to buy a different vehicle altogether. It is the taxpayer's choice. I suspect, and this is what I have found in my dealings with my own constituents, that people drive the company car under these circumstances because it is still fairly cheap to do so. In fact, using the Hon. Member's example of, I believe he said, $3,100 taxable benefit, if the taxpayer is in a one-third tax bracket, which is a fairly rich one, he is paying $1,000 tax on the $3,100 benefit and at that price the taxpayer is getting a car with all the luxuries and operating expenses that go with it. A $1,000 car today, per annum, is quite cheap. After the individual has finished driving it, the insurance and everything else is included.

Third, the Hon. Member asked about prorating and he is quite right that 12,000 kilometres is a dividing line. The standby charge comes into full force after 12,000 kilometres and the taxpayer prorates his liability under 12,000 kilometres. I think he indicated that his constituent has 10,000 kilometres of use, so he would pay five-sixths of his standby liabilities.
I would ask the Hon. Member to take into consideration that 12,000 kilometres is a dividing line that we think is fair to everyone, that personal use is the choice of the taxpayer and that, even so, it is quite an inexpensive way to get a car; and finally, it is prorated below 12,000 kilometres.

Mr. Chairman, I also want to move on to other Clauses. We moved an amendment that has the impact of reducing the number of items taken into expenses for the calculation of what is, in effect, about a 300 per cent tax increase. I suggest that it is reasonable for the Government to give more consideration to that idea than it has up to this point.
I have three short questions. We have suggested to the Government during our discussions that it is unfair for the value of the original price of a car to remain the same year after year, because when an automobile is used for one year or two years, or for 100,000 kilometres, its value declines. Yet the Government wants to tax the user as if it were still a brand-new automobile. Has the Minister reconsidered that principle of cutting down on the valuation?

Mr. Chairman, there was an amendment which I believe was put by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South. 1 cannot recall whether we have actually disposed of that amendment as yet. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South indicates that we have disposed of that motion. If the Hon. Member for Calgary West really wants to move along to a new Section, as he has indicated, I respectfully suggest that we really should not be discussing items which we have not only dealt with but voted on.

May I repeat the question? Will the Government consider changing the value of that automobile each year? As its value declines the taxpayer must pay for personal use based on the value of the automobile. Why should the taxpayer have to pay the same amount in the third year as he would have to pay in the first year when, in fact, the value of the automobile has declined?
Mr. Chairman, I want to go on record as saying that I do not think it is useful for this Committee to entertain discussion of matters that have been dealt with and voted on by the Committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Calgary West could clarify the matter which he is raising now for the benefit of the Chair and the House. The Hon. Minister of State for Finance contends that the Hon. Member for Calgary West is debating an issue which is contained in a Clause which the House has already disposed
Income Tax
of. It would be useful for the Chair if the Hon. Member for Calgary West would clarify that point.

Mr. Chairman, it shows some confusion that exists in the Minister's mind from time to time. We are on Clause 1 which deals with the method of calculation of the benefit to a taxpayer. Part of that method of calculation is the value of the automobile, the value of the expenses and so on. The Committee has disposed of a specific amendment which we presented and which would have changed part of that calculation. To that extent the Minister is correct.
However, the subject matter is Clause 1 and the amendment thereto. The amendment which we are currently debating deals with the calculation on the expense side. The strong feeling that we have that that calculation should be changed could, in fact, be modified somewhat if the Government indicated a willingness to change the calculation on the value side. However, the Government clearly does not even want to talk about it. It does not want Canadian taxpayers to know about it or even its backbenchers to know about it.
We will leave the question of the value of the automobile because the Minister will not answer it. Let us proceed to the expense calculation. The impact of our amendment would be to reduce the expenses simply to the fuel used. There are some parts to that expense method that simply run against the grain because they are wrong.
Why does the Minister insist on charging a private taxpayer a portion of an expense amount for private use which is calculated on an insurance benefit that is based on commercial rates? Every taxpayer in this country knows that a taxi driver pays enormous amounts of money for personal insurance on that automobile. Premiums of $3,000 and $4,000 are not unusual. Private individuals who use an automobile for personal use can purchase insurance for $500 to $700. Simply because my company must pay a high insurance rate, why should I have to receive a taxable benefit based on that commercial insurance payment rather than something related to what I would have to pay to insure my vehicle privately? Why does the Government insist on inflating my tax liability based on that expense item called insurance?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I suppose that the question raised by the Hon. Member is one of degree. It seems to me that when we evaluate these individual costs, we can probably go through the operation of an automobile and find some costs that are more expensive, as I am sure he will find, and some that are less expensive because an employer is supplying them instead of the private individual.
The Government is trying to take a simple course of action for the calculation of these costs. I suggest that the most straightforward answer to his question is simplicity. If the individual calculates these costs and then prorates for personal use, he has a very simple calculation to make and that ends it. On the other hand, I would again want to come back to the principle which is the most important principle of all. It is up to the private individual to decide whether he wants to use the car or find some other method of transportation. If the

individual finds that an extra few dollars on an insurance policy is onerous, then perhaps the individual could calculate the alternatives available. As well, the individual could calculate what other taxpayers pay in particular circumstances. For example, there are those taxpayers who use private vehicles for company business and who charge kilometrage to their employer rather than using the company car. The same example would apply there.

It becomes more and more frustrating. We have moved from principles of equity and fairness and all of a sudden there is simplicity. The principles of Canadian tax law change before our very eyes day after day. It is simple to say that every taxpayer in the country who uses a company automobile for personal purposes will deem the insurance costs to be $600, and they will have to calculate in that portion that the Government decides they should. That is simple, Mr. Parliamentary Secretary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Right.

It is totally unfair that a person on my left who works for a company whose insurance fleet coverage is so bad that they are paying $5,000 for each vehicle will have to pay more tax than somebody on my right who drives the same car, the same everything, but whose fleet coverage is very good with a $3,000 insurance premium per vehicle.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is not true.
That is unfair.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Use your head and start thinking.

Why does the Government have the following formula built into this Bill? The value of the automobile is fixed on the date of purchase and lasts for five years. If the car costs $10,000 at the outset, the Government says that car is still worth $10,000 five years from now. We all know that is nonsense but that is simplicity in the Government's terms. We also know one other thing about that five-year period of time. Repair costs go up. As the vehicle is used more and more and gets older, repair costs increase. A taxpayer with a five-year-old vehicle will be paying more tax dollars to the Government of Canada because of that repair side of this equation than the person on my left who has a brand-new vehicle which is worth more, gives better service and has less problems. That is the Government's idea of simplicity, Mr. Chairman.
Can the Parliamentary Secretary tell me why he wants it both ways? The only logical explanation that I can conceive of is that this is a money grab. It has nothing to do with simplicity, fairness or anything else except a money grab. It is unfair to Canadian taxpayers. Will the Government consider taking the repair part of this taxation liability out of the equation? If the Government is going to keep that automobile value as if it were brand-new, why does the Government not also assume the car needs no repairs? Brand-new vehicles do not need
repairs; they are under warranty. If that is the value the Government is putting on one side of the equation, why does the Government not drop the repair side?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member has a fascinating theory.
Fascinating?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is a theory that I think ordinary practice will not bear out. He is concerned about questions of equity. Bear in mind the simple principle that we are asking people who use their cars for personal use to pay for that use in after-tax dollars. That is the principle. Can the ordinary taxpayer who does not have a company car but has his own car work out some complicated depreciation plan the way the Hon. Member is suggesting? Can this ordinary taxpayer come to the Government and say: "Government, my car is three years old this year; therefore, I want to write some of it off and get a benefit?" The ordinary taxpayer cannot do that. What we are asking is that the personal use of a vehicle be paid for in aftertax dollars and that business-related use be paid for in pre-tax dollars.
Let me carry the Hon. Members' example one step further. He said that there are questions of equity on maintenance. Let us explore that to its logical extreme. If the Hon. Member is counting angels on top of a pin, I will too.
Let us take an individual who has a personal car and drives it on an authorized basis for company use. The longer he hangs on to that car, the more his repair bills will be. Should we allow that individual a complicated set of calculations? No. All we do is say to him that he can collect a kilometrage charge from his employer on a tax-free basis. We do not want to make his life more complicated. We do not come to him and say: "This is the first year of the life of the vehicle, therefore, it can only be so much but the second year will be so much plus some and the third year will be even more". We do not do those kinds of silly calculations. We just say to the individual taxpayer that when his car is for personal use, pay for it with after-tax dollars. When his car is for business use, the car is treated on a tax-exempt basis. It is very simple and very straightforward.
I would like to tell the Hon. Member that I have received a letter which I will show to him. It concerns his behaviour here. This letter is from a chartered accountant, not a constituent of mine. He says that we should be charging the Hon. Member for elementary accounting lessons, and I think that is right. We cannot charge him for the time he has wasted in the House with these silly examples, but at least the Hon. Member should have the decency to pay us for his basic education.
Oh, oh!
You are so arrogant you should be in the Cabinet.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. The Hon. Member for Calgary West.
March 15, 1983

Mr. Chairman, the Government intends to throttle this House later this day. This is amazing. First, the Government moves closure on the Bill. We have time allocation. Suddenly we see Liberal Members standing up and taking the time of the House. Not only do they cut the Opposition's debating time to a day, but the Government cuts that day in half through that kind of behaviour and no doubt we shall get filibustering from the Minister too.
Let me come back to the issue, Mr. Chairman. I, as an individual taxpayer, can decide whether to buy an automobile that is five years old. I pay less for it and I understand that I will probably have larger repair bills. I can make the opposite economic decision and buy a new automobile with full knowledge that I will pay less in repair bills. The Government is saying that if I work for a company, and for whatever set of reasons it is more convenient to use that company automobile part of the time for personal use, I will not have the choice. If I own the automobile I can decide to repair it. If I get a fender bumped a little bit and there is a dent and I do not have the money for the repair, I do not have to repair it. If the company decides to repair it, then under this provision I have to pay tax. That is the basic unfairness.
We are being charged as though we owned a new automobile when, in fact, it is not a new automobile. Then we are being charged for all the repairs which the company decides to make on it. The individual's choice has disappeared. This is totally unfair and I urge Members opposite to vote for the amendment which the Hon. Member for Mississauga South has moved because his amendment at least puts some sense of fairness back into the system.

On Clauses 8, 9 and 128(12)-

March 15, 1983
Income Tax

Mr. Chairman, this give us an opportunity to look at some of the background of the Small Business Bond. I have a number of questions about it because of the way the situation has evolved. Since the concept of the bond was introduced in the Crosbie budget in 1979 it has proved to be an interesting and in some cases a very good and reasonable measure for businesses to expand initially or in cases of financial distress, to refinance.
I should like to express some concern that it is available only in cases of bail-out for those who are in financial distress now and that we do not have the opportunity to use the mechanism for people who want to expand.
I wonder what the rationale of the Government was in changing the concept from one of assisting expansion to one of assisting those in financial distress. I understand the difference between the Small Business Development Bond and the Small Business Bond, but what financial parameters were used to decide that it was no longer in the best interest of businesses to allow them to use this to expand and instead use it only as a bail-out mechanism?
Does the Government know the cost compared to the benefit to the Government through taxation, increased employment opportunities, business expansions and so on? 1 know the Government can relate to a lost-tax position, but can it compare that to the expansion that took place and the additional economic activity that took place?

Mr. Speaker, I will begin by adopting the comments of the Elon. Member for Bruce-Grey that the section was of help to many small businesses. The amount of take-up by small businesses and banks has been very encouraging, not only under the original section, but as well subsequent to the amendments which are in this section. Advantage has been taken of them since the announcement was made.
One of the complaints about this provision initially was that it applied only to unincorporated business entities. One of the amendments before us is to expand that to unincorporated sole proprietorships, thereby opening the provision to a larger number of Canadian businessmen.
In response to the question raised by the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey, I should point out that we felt that, as well as applying this to the unincorporated person, we should include those in financial difficulty.
Realizing that this section was limited in scope, the Government was relying upon the participation of the banking institutions to assist business. Considering the amount of funds available to assist in this area, and bearing in mind that there was no take-up under the provision, it was felt that the Government had to target on those businesses in more serious difficulty and those which, without funding under this provision, would otherwise fail. The provision for expansion seemed to address the most needy of small businesses, those close to using this provision as a last resort. Under the circumstances we felt that that was a group that really should be addressed first.
As I say, with the limited resources that the banks would use in this vehicle, we thought that the money should go first of all to those who, without the money, would not be able to continue.

Basically, I do not disagree with the idea that there needed to be an extension of this to those who are unincorporated, and that if there are limited resources they should be made available to those most in need.
However, the Minister, probably because I was not clear enough, has not responded to the basic question as to why the expansion orientation of this whole mechanism, which was implicit in the original suggestion, was changed so that it is now only useful to those who are in financial distress. That is irrespective of the amount of available resources. What parameters were used or what was the basis for the Government stating "This is costing us too much", or "It will not work this way", or whatever the rationale was, so that now we need to change it only for those in financial distress, in contrast to allowing it to be used for expansion and letting enterprise develop with the use of it?
I would also make one final and quick point. From time to time we on this side argued very strongly and, in the end, achieved the effect of making it available to unincorporated as well as incorporated farms. However, at the time that it was useful for expansion, only those who were incorporated were able to use it. The program initially had the effect of forcing people, if they were to expand, to become incorporated. The argument used at that time by the tax Department in stating that it really could not handle this very well unless people were incorporated is really denied by the fact that it is now used for unincorporated businesses. What was the real basis for saying that it could not use this for expansion any more?

Mr. Chairman, the officials advised me that it was the recognition of the fact that the scheme was limited in terms of the amount of money available to any business, whether it was business to be used for investment or to be used in the case of failure-those businesses which were not concerned about expanding, but were concerned about continuing on because of the state of their balance sheets.
We recognized the fact that there was only limited future funding available because of the remarkable take-up in the first year or so. The Government therefore recognized that we had to make some choices and that with those limited resources available we should attempt to direct assistance to the businesses which, without this help, would have failed.
That was our first concern. I admit, in so doing, that we therefore precluded the initial use by businessmen which had been for investment purposes. However, it was assistance to those most in need, bearing in mind our information from the banks that the amount of funds had been, by and large, remarkably taken down. The access of the banks to this vehicle had, by and large, been exhausted.
March 15, 1983

We are coming very close to the question now. What is the practical limitation on the ability of the banks to use this? Obviously, bank profits are healthy. My understanding of the basic mechanism is that for tax purposes they are able to transfer their profits into a dividend pay-out. Therefore, what is the limitation? In addition, what would be the judgment of the Government as to whether it is really costing the Government money in terms of tax revenue as compared to additional economic activity generated by those businesses which would expand?

Mr. Chairman, I believe the Hon. Member asked the question in a form which really pinpoints the issue. This vehicle would be available to banks only if they were in a taxable position.
Hon. Members will recall that last year the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs began an analysis of bank profits. Six months after the study was under way, with the downturn in the economy, rather than concern over bank profits there was concern over the ability of banks to make profits in the very weakened economic climate. As a result the Committee, instead of returning with recommendations as to how the banks should divvy up their excess profits, stated its concerns over the ability of banks to continue to serve their purpose under the original legislation in the country. It recommended that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, for example, be enhanced and that the original security of $20,000 for depositors under the legislation be increased to $60,000, which reflected some concern over the ability of the banks and financial community to serve Canadians in a depressed economy. Again, that was reflected in the banks' taxable position. Toward the end of 1982, it was very apparent that their taxable position was deteriorating because their profits were deteriorating.
The first quarter of 1983 has shown another bounce and the ball is going the other way, we hope. However, it is too soon, in this quarter, for us to judge whether that is a trend which will accelerate and, in fact, what the taxable position will be. If that trend continues through the rest of the year, it is conceivable that the Government may in the future decide that the restriction to serving only those businesses in financial difficulty should be rethought. However, on our best projections, considering the picture for 1982 and projections into the first quarter of this year, that is not what we perceived would be the case. For the time being, therefore, we think that we should maintain the section and this program which is directed, first, to those who would end up on the bankruptcy casualty list without it.
Would the Chair help me? How much time do I have left in which to speak?
Infinite.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member began speaking at 12.05 p.m. He is allowed 20 minutes.

I would direct a further question to the Minister. If there are figures, I think it would be useful to place
Income Tax
them on the record in relation to the Government's position as to cost of lost revenue compared with additional economic activity created. Again, various figures from different sources have been stated for the record, and I think it would be helpful to get an idea of the Government's position.
The second question which I would like to pose for the Minister relates to the way in which the tax Department will treat these cases, whether it will involve the original situation or the current type of situation of distress. There is real concern that these matters be considered by the tax Department, not so much in the case of expansion, but, more particularly, in situations of distress.
As time goes on and, hopefully, businesses are in sounder shape and things are going better for them, the tax Department might say: "All right, you obtained the bond, but you really did not qualify for it because you were not that badly off'. I think a number of applications have been tested or considered by the corporate sector in an attempt to find out whether some kind of pre-judgment could be given. What sense of confidence is there that there will not, in fact, be a number of those cases which will not be accepted by the tax Department on the basis that there was really no justification at the time?

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member really asks two questions. He reverted to the question he asked previously. The Department does not have a precise answer to the amount of economic activity that was generated by the plan. They believe there is no way they could give that figure with precision. I can, though, confirm that the take-down of the plan was over $2 billion worth of support for small businesses.
On the second question, if implicit in the question is the consideration of whether this Section should be reopened so as to make it available to those companies which are looking for expansion as they did previously, or to avoid the funds being used now for financial difficulty situations where there will be a remarkable turn around in short order, I think all I can say is that the Department will continue to monitor the take-down of the funding. No doubt the general economic indicators of the Department will also signal to the Department whether the Section should be reconsidered.

Mr. Chairman, when the tax Department is looking at a particular case, or at the involvement of different shareholders in a particular company, for instance, there are a whole range of things that could happen that would bring into question the legitimacy of their original application. I can see a lot of opportunity for confusion, dispute and difficulty in a particular situation where there may be ten different people on a board of directors. In a small community, or even in a large community, I think this is likely to happen. Someone who is intimately involved with a particular application may also be involved either in the same way or in a peripheral way with some other application. I wonder if there are any general

March 15, 1983
Income Tax
guidelines that the Minister could indicate right now, or could he tell us how rigidly and how strictly is that kind of arm's length approach going to be applied when it comes time for tax consideration?

Mr. Chairman, I guess that really gets down to the decision of officials in the Department of Revenue who would be administering the law and the rulings under this Section as to whether businesses comply or not. I am advised by the officials that there is some procedure for obtaining a preliminary opinion whether a company in a particular situation did meet all of the criteria. Presumably information on all of the peripheral things that the Hon. Member has talked about would be made available to the officials in the Department and, having that in mind, if they make an initial ruling based on all of the available information at that time, the Department would not change its mind later on. The question of whether the Section should be changed later on or not is something different.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The Hon. Member's time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, if I could follow up the remarks and questions from my colleague from Bruce-Grey, I believe the Minister stated that a total amount of $2 billion had been approved in loans, and I would assume this would mean the Government had guaranteed that amount, which was loaned, of course, by the chartered banks. Is that right? There was no guarantee?
That is not a provision of the Section, Mr. Chairman, and it is not a practice of the Government.

Mr. Chairman, I would ask the Minister if there are any figures as to how much of that $2 billion was loaned by the chartered banks before the new restriction came in that only to those in need would the money be available. I am curious about that amount.
Also, when the original small Business Development Bond was brought in by, I believe, the Crosbie budget-and I commend this present Government for carrying on with it-at that particular time it was restricted to small limited companies. I am just wondering if it would not be better to go back to the original plan where there would be more money available, because now, as I understand it, it is only for those in need. I have had several of my constituents come to me and say that they were in dire circumstances and needed money and they asked if they could avail themselves of this Small Business Development Bond. Of course, I would point out to them that they would have to go to the chartered banks and present their financial statements. In the great majority of cases, they were turned down. The banks said that they knew that they were in need of money but that they were in such serious need of money that the banks would not lend it to them. This to me is far from fair. I will admit that money cannot be loaned to a bankruptcy but there are a great many people who could have got this money but were turned down.
My question to the Minister, first of all, is how much was loaned before and how much after?

Mr. Chairman, under the original provision I am told there was over $2 billion used by small businesses through the banking system. Since the provision was expanded on the one hand and also directed toward financial difficulty or dire straits situations, there has been somewhat over a $200 million taken down. In the example given by the Hon. Member, I do not follow the Hon. Member's logic. If indeed the person who has asked for help is a person described by the Hon. Member as being in dire straits, presumably he is the very person whom the amended Section helping people in difficulty is directed toward. He is the person who would now qualify. It is only a person who wants to expand, who is looking to grow, who does not have that present urgency and dire situation that the Hon. Member refers to, who would now not qualify.

Mr. Chairman, what I was pointing out was that there are certain businesses which are on the verge of bankruptcy. There are a great many firms that are hanging in and are able to keep their heads above water, even in this economic climate, and I will go back six months ago when the economic situation was even gloomier than it looks at the present time. There were certain strong businesses then which wanted to expand, wanted to consolidate, yet were not eligible.
It is an old military axiom that success and not weakness should be reinforced. I understand that the banks have put up $200 million. I would be interested in knowing how many of those loans went sour; in other words, where they were trying to prop up weakness.

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member's question is really supplementary to that of the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey. We looked at what the choices were, and since the provision was designed to be administered through the chartered banks, we knew it was dependent upon their profit and tax situation. We knew the provision had been widely used and very successfully, but the available funding was drying up.
Faced with that circumstance, the Government proposed that assistance should go to those the Hon. Member described as being in dire straits. He used a figure of speech in military operations-that you support your strengths. In the military sense, you must also assist the wounded. The military does not abandon the wounded.
Obviously we have to be concerned about those who, without this help, would have been clients for bankruptcy court. We felt that under the circumstances we had to assist those who, without this kind of help, would have been in real difficulty. We are hopeful that with the upturn in the economy those who are strong will be assisted by it and will not require assistance from the Government.

Mr. Chairman, I again come back to the percentages. The banks have only loaned one-tenth as much to
March 15, 1983

those in a serious financial position compared to the old basis. It was loaned to those with an okay credit rating, those who could very well repay the loan.
I agree with the Minister that we must assist those small businesses that are in a very serious situation. I emphasize again that many small businesses could have been saved if the Government had gone to the banks and tried to work something out for those businesses that were close to the wall. I do not have to remind the Minister of the great number of bankruptcies that have been announced; it is common knowledge. Many could have been prevented if the Small Business Development Bond was available to them. However, they reached the stage where they were just hanging on while the banks were giving them consideration. When the final line was drawn, they were turned down and went into bankruptcy.
With the upturn in the economy, is the Minister going to recommend to his colleagues that the Small Business Development Bond be available to individuals and companies so that they can enlarge and modernize? That would result in more people being taken off the unemployment rolls. It would be a good deal for the Government as well as the individual businessman or small limited company. There would not only be savings with regard to payment of unemployment benefits, but the Government would start collecting income tax and other taxes as well. 1 hope the Minister has some good news for us on this. Is there anything in the offing to the effect that this money will be available through the Small Business Development Bond to other than those in dire straits?

Mr. Chairman, the best news would be that the economy was performing so well that the Government would not be required to provide assistance to any businessman. It would be perking without this drain against Government resources.
There is something Hon. Members should consider when comparing situations. First, with regard to the planned program for expansion assistance-assisting those in dire straits as described by the Hon. Member-the expansionary use of the bond was for a period exceeding two years. That is in comparison to the new provision which has only been in place for six months. He has to keep that in mind.
Second, I responded to the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey that the Government will monitor the results of this program. I cannot say what the Government will do except to say that it was as a result of an analysis of the use of the program, the fact that the taxable income was not there for the banks and there was a limited use of this Section. Therefore, we had to make some changes. The Government will continue to monitor it. Whether changes in the Section are warranted will depend on the performance of the economy.

Mr. Chairman, would the Minister or his officials make a guesstimate that with the more favourable financial outlook for the banks, which had a better year this year, they will be more sympathetic to loans under the Small Business Development Bond, or will it not make any difference? I believe it was half prime plus 1 or 2 per cent at which
Income Tax
the bonds were negotiated and the money loaned. The bank would not have to declare this in its profits because of the greatly reduced interest rate it provided to these special customers. Does the Minister have an optimistic view of more use of the Small Business Development Bond in the new climate?

Mr. Chairman, I could give many qualifiers as to why my answer could not be optimistic, but I am by nature optimistic. I am optimistic that the banks will be able to offer the program, but I cannot speak for the banks. The Hon. Member referred to their having a better year. They have had a better first quarter this year over last. The banks will obviously watch their own performance in making their decision.

I appreciate that it is the first quarter, but at least it is looking better. Do either the Minister or his officials have a breakdown of the money loaned under the new plan, whether to partnerships or individuals as against limited companies, as was the case originally? I am curious to know whether a lot of individuals have been able to take advantage of it, or is it still by and large mostly small, private companies that have it?
Mr. Chairman, that is a very good question. I do not have the answer available this morning. I will undertake to see if this information is available and make it known to the Hon. Member.

Mr. Chairman, the amount of $2 billion was mentioned. I am not clear on this. Was the legislation under the old set-up amended where individual entrepreneurs could qualify on the expansion basis, not on the need basis? If so, how much of the $2 billion went to incorporated companies and how much was available to sole proprietors or individual businessmen, such as farmers, etc.?

Mr. Chairman, the provision which was in place for expansion, which is the $2 billion plus I referred to, was available only to incorporated entities and, therefore, the total amount was used under those circumstances.

Mr. Chairman, I have one further question. It is actually not a question but, shall we say, a plea. In other words, the ordinary individual businessman or small proprietors, such as partners who are not incorporated, have not been able to take advantage of the Small Business Development Bond as it was originally planned by this Government as well as the previous Conservative Government. The only individuals who have been able to take advantage of that have been those with their backs to the wall, who were in really serious financial trouble, and no reasonably successful proprietorships have been able to qualify or have been able to have an application granted.

Mr. Chairman, I will consider the Hon. Member's plea as a representation. As I have indicated, the bond was originally only available to incorporated entities. The

March 15, 1983
Income Tax
law has now been changed to include sole proprietorships. In any further amendments or alterations to the program we will seriously consider the representations of the Hon. Member.

Mr. Chairman, I find it interesting and puzzling that the Minister uses as his explanation for the change in the Act, which means that money will not be available to borrow for expansion or development, the argument that the Government wanted to use the relatively limited amount of money which was available for those companies which were in danger of going bankrupt. I find it puzzling, Mr. Chairman, because of the billions of dollars in loans and grants which the Government has been able to give to some very large corporations, such as Dome Petroleum, Chrysler and Maislin Industries, the Government's argument that it has a limited amount of money for small business.
I find interesting the Minister's explanation that the banks were limited because they did not have such a good year last year. Well, we know that in the first quarter of this year bank profits were up by 41 per cent, and we know that because of the tax system which this Government has implemented over the years bank taxes are down, if the banks pay any taxes at all-and there are one or two which last year paid no taxes. The rate of tax is down to about the same rate as individual taxpayers in the lowest tax bracket.
The program before it was changed was very successful. It was lauded by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, which has expressed some very serious objections to and criticisms of the change in the Small Business Development Bond to the new system. The Ministry has said that the new system provides for the Small Business Bonds and permits loans to be made to unincorporated businesses, but according to the Canadian Federation of Independent Business it has been used almost exclusively by farmers. Small, unincorporated businesses have not availed themselves of this to any extent. Indeed, the loans made are well down in number.
Given the fact, Mr. Chairman, according to some figures released yesterday and today, that last month we had the second highest number of business bankruptcies ever in this country, it seems to me pretty obvious that the program is not working. I would like to ask the Minister to explain, not just to me but to the people who belong to the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, why the ability to loan money for expansion was removed from the new program.

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member used the example of Government assistance to firms such as Chrysler through the guarantee program to that firm, saying that if we can do it for Chrysler, why can we not offer some assistance to small-businessmen. In my experience, Mr. Chairman, although Chrysler Corporation has large plants and employs large numbers of people in the manufacturing plants, they are served right across this country by hundreds of smaller firms, including sole proprietorships, smaller partnerships and small-businessmen. The automobile industry is not just a large plant in operation. It was for that reason that the Government decided to offer the guarantees to Chrysler, because there were
representations made at the time when Chrysler was in serious difficulty for support, as I say, not only for the larger plants but for people right across the country who saw their livelihood going down the tube if Chrysler folded. I personally received dozens of representations from people not only in my constituency but in many other constituencies when that was a hot issue two and a half years ago.
I believe it is simplistic to say that the assistance which has been provided to some of the larger firms has been designed to assist just the large corporations. It helps the small people, the small businesses and single proprietors. It is also simplistic to say that this provision is the only way in which, conversely, the Government provides direct assistance to small businesses or to the smaller players in the economy. For example, the preferred rate of 25 per cent to small businesses is a benefit to the small business sector which, taken cumulatively, is worth over a billion dollars to that sector of the economy. Therefore, we are providing assistance in many ways other than the particular Section before us.
I cannot comment on the accuracy of the figures which have been given by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North because, as I have indicated, our Department does not have that breakdown. The Hon. Member indicated he has figures which show that the take-up was by farmers almost exclusively. I do not have the figures to weigh that comment, but certainly it was available to all other sectors. The provision was available to other people who wanted to use it.

Mr. Chairman, I was not suggesting for a moment that the Government should not have made loans to Chrysler, to Massey-Ferguson or to other companies which are involved in the production of goods, some of which are exported. What I am saying is that it seems obvious to me there is a vast difference in the way in which the Government approaches requests for assistance from large corporations and the way in which it approaches requests for assistance from small businesses.
It has been pointed out frequently that 65 per cent of the jobs in this country are provided by small businesses. When we see the record rate of bankruptcies which have occurred for the last two years, every month more bankruptcies than in the same month a year earlier, we have to be concerned.
I point out to the Minister that while there may have been some justification for loan guarantees to productive companies like Chrysler, according to The Financial Times Canadian banks made loans of $4.2 billion to a few large corporations for takeovers. Many of these takeovers added nothing to the productive capacity of this country and most of the loans have now been classed as non-productive loans, which means that the companies are not even paying the interest let alone the principal. So I say to the Minister that there is a vast difference between the way this Government and the banks look at the problems of large coporations and those of small corporations.
March 15, 1983

As far as the point I have made that the new bonds are being used mainly by farmers is concerned, that information came to me, as I am sure it did to the Minister's office, as a result of a survey by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business which showed conclusively that the new bond was not being used to the same extent as the Small Business Development Bond.
The Minister has not answered my question, and that of other Members, which was simply this. There are small businesses which are not going bankrupt, which have survived this recession. They are in a position to expand and modernize. They want to be able to use the bond as they previously did, to buy new equipment, to modernize and expand. Yet just at this time when, hopefully-and 1 am not as hopeful as some Members-we have turned the corner and the recession is over-because there are some signs of improvement-the Government cuts these small-businessmen off by saying it will no longer permit them to borrow money as they did under the Small Business Development Bond program.

Mr. Chairman, I would have to repeat the gist of my last answer to the Hon. Member when he says that the Government has dealt with the two sectors in a different manner. The support of firms such as Chrysler was not just because the Government was directing assistance to so-called large firms. It was because we recognize that the large firm is just one part of a large industry and that many small-businessmen right across this country are involved in the manufacture of parts for those vehicles. That in itself is an industry. Many of these people are sales people, small firms, small operators, small garages and outlets, and they were all in jeopardy. It was not just the so-called big Chrysler operation, there were many small-businessmen who stood to lose if the Government had not moved to provide that guarantee. If the Hon. Member uses the example of Chrysler to support the contention that the Government has dealt with the two sectors in a different way, then I disagree with him most emphatically.
As to the other point, Mr. Chairman, it was raised by two Members earlier in the proceedings. We have indicated that the Government was faced with a choice. There were limited resources available under the program and we decided we should direct the assistance to those who need it the most. The Hon. Member tells me that surveys show that farmers took advantage of it to a greater extent than did other small-businessmen. All I can say is that I hope other sectors in the small business category do not need the program or will not have to call on it in the future. I hope that is the case.

Mr. Chairman, we are discussing Clause 8 and Clause 9 which deal with the Small Business Bonds. I am wondering if the Hon. Minister can tell us in short order how many loans have been granted under each of these two categories and the amount of money involved. Earlier he referred to a figure of $2 billion which, since the most recent changes, has dropped down to $200 million.

Mr. Chairman, my officials advise that the $200 million I referred to earlier was used under both Clause 8 and Clause 9. I do not have a breakdown of how much is attributable to each. My officials indicate that we can get that information and I will make it available to the Hon. Member.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure everyone here would be interested in that. Will the Minister give us his view as to why there was $2 billion lent under the original Section and only $200 million since the changes? What does the Minister feel occurred in the economy to result in such a dramatic change?

Mr. Chairman, if we look at the performance of the economy since the introduction of the initial Section in 1979 and the performance of the economy in the last 24 or 30 months, obviously the economy was performing very strongly immediately following the original program. More recently the economy has deteriorated, as have all the economies of the industrialized world. So while businessmen were looking at expansion at one time, in the last little while they were looking at survival.

Mr. Chairman, from a political perspective, we note that the original Section was brought forward under the Conservative Government and the new one was brought forward under the Liberal Government, along with a dramatic downturn in the economy.

subsubtopic: CANAGREX-NECESSITY FOR EARLY ADOPTION OF BILL C-85
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it was reported in the press recently that a resolution of the National Council had risen from the ashes of the Parti Quebecois to

March 15, 1983
warn the farmers of Quebec against the danger of Bill C-85 to establish a corporation called Canagrex. Nevertheless, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Agricultural Producers' Union and the majority of groups interested in the growth of the agri-food sector are in favour of the Bill, and it should have been adopted long ago.

subtopic: FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR CALGARY WINTER OLYMPICS
FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR CALGARY WINTER OLYMPICS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister responsible for Sport in Canada stated on October 22, 1982, that the federal Government had committed $200 million to the Calgary Olympic Games and that $500,000 had then been advanced to Calgary on its commitment.
Despite the fact that the Quebec provincial game "Hockey Select" was already under way, he vowed that Calgary would receive its $200 million one way or another.
At Committee stage on Bill C-95, the Provinces indicated a willingness to negotiate a sharing of that commitment. It has always been open to the Canadian Olympic Association or other appropriate sports organizations to make a proposal under which that body would operate a sports pool or lottery.
I want to assure the Canadian Olympic Association and Calgary that, if this Party were writing the cheques, an instalment form of payment out of general revenues would be already in place so as to ensure the success of the Calgary Games. Why does the Government not live up to its commitment and worry about the sports pool later?

maintopic: REFUSAL OF AID TO HIGH SCHOOL BASKETBALL TEAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I find it disturbing and depressing that the Department of Fitness and Amateur Sport finds itself regulated to the point that it cannot give
some financial support to an amateur high school basketball team competing in an international tournament in the United States.
In my riding of Hamilton West the Cathedral High School boys' senior basketball team finished off a remarkable season with an invitation to the prestigious Catholic Invitational Tournament held annually in Cumberland, Maryland, in the vicinity of Washington, D.C. This is an annual event to which the eight most outstanding Catholic high school basketball teams in the United States are invited. This year, for the first time in the history of the tournament, a Canadian team has been accorded the honour of being invited to participate.
This school has won all tournaments in which it has participated during the year. On the basis of this performance, it has been selected as a worthy representative in the tournament in the United States on March 17.
Being a Catholic high school in the Province of Ontario, there are no provincial funds to support the school, either academically or in the field of athletics. Any trips involving teams from this school are largely funded privately, and a trip to Washington is a costly event.
The Department of Fitness and Amateur Sport should show some flexibility in handling money in its budget. It should not be restricted by rigid regulations administered by bureaucrats. A deserving team representing this country in international events could be encouraged, and amateur sport promoted, by a grant from the federal Government. I wish Cathedral High School every success in this prestigious tournament.

Madam Speaker, the federal Government is tightening the noose on post secondary education in Canada by limiting future spending to six and five.
It is another illustration of the Government's shortsightedness-cutting funds to the very institutions most vital to our economic recovery, to research and development, and to the training of a highly skilled Canadian work force.
Canadian colleges and universities have been subjected to severe financial cutbacks for the past ten years, while student enrolment, due to severe unemployment, has increased. Canadian youth, unemployed at a rate of 22.5 per cent, are not only denied jobs but are now denied access to a decent education.
The federal Government has abdicated its responsibility to foster educational goals, as outlined two years ago by the then Secretary of State, now the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox). The federal Government cries for greater accountability in funding education, but offers no concrete proposals to achieve this. Indeed, in dropping its fiscal transfers to the six and five formula, it robs the universities and colleges of $102 million for the coming year, and has given no indication of how this money will be spent.
The New Democratic Party calls on the Government to engage in urgent negotiations with the Provinces, universities and colleges, to restructure the current system of funding of post-secondary education before irreparable damage is done to the universities and colleges of Canada.

Madam Speaker, reports from Poland of arrests and the continuing military suppression of Solidarity, a union which embodies the hopes and aspirations of the Polish people, seem to be never ending.

The scarcity of both time and money, along with the fact that the immediate crisis in Poland had eased somewhat and there was, consequently less Canadian reaction to report, all combined to make the decision necessary.
I am not satisfied with this response. The scarcity of both time and money is not a viable reason for the CBC's cut. GRASS!E POST OFFICE CENTENNIAL

Madam Speaker, many times I have stood in this House to point out the inefficiencies of the Canadian postal system. Delays in delivery and unjustified increases in postage rates have many times been dealt with from this seat. Today I intend to deal with yet another aspect of the Canada Post story.
In my riding there is a small community called Grassie, in the Township of West Lincoln. The Postmaster in this community, Mr. Carl Thomas, operates a general store in addition to his postal duties. Herein lies the problem.
Mr. Thomas and his family have operated this store and post office for the past half century. Here we have a faithful public servant whose ancestors were the people who built this country. He has gone quietly about his daily work without thanks or recognition, for many, many years. Yet, as Mr. Thomas's elected representative, I have no opportunity to offer my congratulations in the House of Commons when he is about to celebrate the one hundredth anniversary of the founding of his post office on March 31, 1983. Instead, I shall be compelled to send him a letter outlining my sincere best wishes and hopes for a happy and prosperous future. Is this fair? I think not. But I shall do the right thing and refrain from making any such remarks in the House of Commons, and send the aforementioned letter. Let us hope it gets there.
Hear, hear!
March 15, 1983

CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES-APPLICATION TO FORMER MINISTER, NORMAN CAFIK
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to return to the issue of the conflict of guidelines for Ministers and former Ministers, specifically guidelines A and B. This matter is not settled because the guidelines are not clear and there are further examples that raise serious questions.
Take the case of Norman Cafik. He was defeated in the May, 1979, election. He resigned from the cabinet on June 3, 1979. By September, 1979, press stories had him joining Ebco Industries Ltd. in Vancouver. By December, 1979, according to the British Columbia Companies Office, he was a director of Ebco Industries Ltd. He, as Vice-President, and the President, Mr. Eppich, approached the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce for a grant. Meetings were held with officials and submissions were made. Perhaps it appeared there was lobbying.
The then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Hon. Herb Gray, was briefed. On April 27, 1981, in Richmond, British Columbia, the Minister announced a $6.7 million grant. The pattern is very similar to the Gillespie affair.
Surely the guidelines and the conduct of former Ministers must now be examined by a parliamentary committee.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I have a copy of the agreement dated September 1, 1981, which was signed by the Government of Canada and the Government of Alberta. That agreement says, with reference to prices, that, "The overall average Field price of conventional old oil. .. will not exceed 75 per cent of the actual international price of oil."
The Prime Minister agrees that this means that Canadian prices should track the international price. When the international price goes up, the Canadian price should go up, but it also means that if the international price goes down, the Canadian price should go down.
As of yesterday, the drop in world prices has meant that the Canadian price is now at 84 per cent of the world price level. Will the Minister take steps to enforce this agreement and ensure that it is lived up to, by bringing about a S3 a barrel drop in the price of conventional Canadian oil?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

Madam Speaker, if the Hon. Member reads the whole agreement I think he will know that we have an agreement which changes the price every six months. The next change in price will only be in July.
Of course, as he knows, the Premier of Alberta is of the view that the agreement only meant when the price increased. This means a ceiling when the price decreased.
We take a different point of view and we are discussing that with the Government of Alberta at this time. In fact I will be meeting with the Minister of Energy of Alberta, Mr. Zaozirny, on Friday, in Edmonton.

Madam Speaker, the Minister knows very well that there is a time lag between the wellhead price and the price that the consumer pays. He also knows that, as of today, Canadians are paying prices beyond what this agreement stipulates.
Considering the fact that a $3 a barrel drop in the price of conventional oil would mean a $1.6 billion stimulus to the Canadian economy and 33,000 additional Canadian jobs, according to the federal Government's own calculations, will the Minister take steps today to ensure that that agreement is lived up to and that the needed stimulus for the Canadian economy is provided so that Canadians who are out of work will be able to find jobs?
