subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER COMMITTEE STAGE OF BILL C-139
speechtext:
That, in relation to Bill C-139, an Act to amend the statute law relating to income tax (No. 2), one additional sitting day shall be allotted to the further consideration in Committee of the Whole stage of the said Bill;
That, at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in that sitting, any proceeding before the Committee shall be interrupted, if required, for the purpose of this order and, in turn, every question then necessary in order to dispose of the Committee of the Whole stage of the said Bill shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a motion for time allocation on Bill C-139, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act, which has a background of 18 months and goes back to the period of time of the November, 1981 budget when most of the measures contained in the legislation were first announced. During this long period there have been frequent debates in this House, extensive consultations right across the country with affected segments of the private sector and detailed studies by members not only of the Standing Committee of this House but as well a parallel Committee in the Senate.
The various stages of House debate have consumed 25 sitting days, the equivalent of six full weeks of debate under the new rules, Mr. Speaker, and involving no less than 200 speakers. It became more and more obvious as time went on that the Opposition Parties were deliberately delaying passage of this very important legislation. They have ignored the obvious urgency of having these important measures passed in order to achieve three things: an end to the uncertainty in the business community; provide a legal basis for the payment of millions of dollars in tax refunds; and to clear the way for the introduction of the 1983 budget. For months the Opposition has been following a strategy of forcing the Government to resort to time allocation on very important Bills. We saw this tactic in the operation of the six and five capping legislation, and more recently on the borrowing authority legislation. The Government's request for co-operation and pleas for a reasonable solution have met with continued obstruction.
March 15, 1983

Let me review the record of the past 16 months, Mr. Speaker. Following the introduction of the 1981 budget, we had a full six-day budget debate with 47 speakers. Over the ensuing six months the Government entered into a series of consultations with private sector groups which led to several important modifications in the budget proposal. Various announcements were issued setting out the scope of these modifications.
In April of 1982 an explanatory paper concerning the proposed shift of the sales tax to the wholesale level was issued. A paper on the budget process was tabled. Revised rules on the taxation of charities were made public after consultation with charitable organizations.
In May a document was issued on draft regulations relating to capital cost allowances.
The budget of June, 1982 contained a detailed package of draft income tax legislation which was distributed nationwide for comment by tax law practitioners and interested taxpayers. That budget also announced revised rules on the taxation of life insurance income, including the exempt policy concept which reflected many weeks of consultation with representative groups of the life insurance industry as well as individual companies and many individual agents right across the whole of Canada. Other modifications were announced at the same time affecting such things as the interest expense deduction, the automobile standby charge and the provision for forward averaging of the incomes of athletes and artists. This budget was debated for six days with 51 speakers taking part.
Many comments were received on the draft legislation and in early August the draft was referred to a Special Committee of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. That Committee met through August and September while Parliament was in recess and prepared a detailed study of the legislation after hearing numerous witnesses. A lengthy report was prepared by that Subcommittee and many of the suggestions were subsequently adopted. The proposed legislation was reviewed once more.
An economic statement was delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on October 27. Among other things, the proposal to tax certain employee benefits, including health and dental plans, was dropped. Exemptions were introduced in the taxation of work in progress. The date for implementing the shift in the sales tax was deferred, and the application of new rules for the taxation of charitable organizations was delayed for further study.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, the tax proposals had been under active study, as I indicated, in all those forums for a full 12 months, not to mention the opportunities which the Official Opposition and the NDP took to conduct their own hearings right across the country on the budget legislation.
Finally, on December 7, 1982 Bill C-139 was introduced to encompass all the modifications which had been made. It was accompanied by explanatory notes setting out the intent of the legal language. That was the first time, Mr. Speaker, in the
Time Allocation
history of our tax legislation that such a step had been taken to assist Canadians generally in their understanding of this complicated legislation.
Since the introduction of Bill C-139 we have heard a parade of Opposition speeches, most of them repetitious. On second reading alone we had 99-I repeat, 99-speakers, 74 of them Conservative and 17 from the New Democratic Party. It had been the hope of the Government after all these studies had taken place that the matter could have been dealt with expeditiously by this Parliament. Now, more than three months after its introduction, after all that consultation and opportunity for discussion by Canadians generally, we are still a very long way from obtaining passage in the normal course which we had hoped this Parliament would follow.
At this point I might recall a remark made in the House by the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) on November 10 when he exercised his responsibility as financial critic and demanded to know when the Government was going to bring in tax legislation for the 1981 budget in order to ease the uncertainty of the business community. In retrospect, Mr. Speaker, those were hollow words judging from the performance of the Official Opposition since that time.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the Government indeed is as anxious as was the Conservative Party at one time to end the tax uncertainty. It is anxious indeed to permit the processing and distribution of millions of tax refunds worth over $6 billion which will go to Canadians, some of whom are unemployed. That is the intent of the motion before the House today, Mr. Speaker. That is what we seek to accomplish by this motion.

Mr. Speaker, this is the most disgraceful closure of a Bill we have had before this Parliament. This Party has done its level best to move this Bill forward in Committee of the Whole House. It is a horrendously complicated Bill. It involves nearly 300 pages of the worst kind of draftsmanship one could ever imagine.
So far we have completed nearly one third of the Bill. We have dealt with automobiles, standby charges and the cost of maintenance. We have dealt with professional work in progress. The Government has not dealt with it, we have. We asked the Government to do something for the notaries and the Government refused. The Government has amendments in that respect but it does not want to allow the Bill to stay in the House so those amendments can be presented in the normal course. We have dealt in detail with insurance companies and policy taxation, with annuities and guaranteed investment certificates. We have dealt with capital costs on the demolition of buildings. We are presently dealing with Small Business Development Bonds. However, there is a host of other things which should be dealt with where people in Canada have presented logical arguments as to why there should be change-minor change in many cases-in the Bill. Yet the Government does not want to listen, does not want to proceed, does not want to be honest, but it does want to ram this Bill through without discussion.

March 15, 1983
Time Allocation
It is a disgrace, Mr. Speaker, to the democratic process that the Minister should stand in this House this afternoon and attempt to ram a Bill through by saying it has had ample discussion. He knows it has not. Let us talk about the ample discussion that income tax legislation should have. The Government knows that, in an incarnation with another Minister of Finance, it passed a budget in both 1977 and 1978. When this Party had the opportunity to form the Government for a limited period of time during 1979, we presented to this House an income tax Bill of not quite 100 pages. That Bill was brought to a Committee of the Whole House. There was really only one difficulty with it and that was the provision for a special rate of tax of 33 per cent for service corporations. The budgets of 1977 and 1978 were approved by a Liberal Government but the tax Bills that resulted from those budgets were presented by a Conservative Government. Closure was not imposed by that Conservative Government. The Bill was debated in Committee of the Whole House for five days. Both sides considered that to be reasonable.
In the case of the Bill before the House, there have been four days and two hours of debate on a horrendously complicated piece of legislation which deals with the most changes to the Income Tax Act since 1971. The Government claims that the House has spent too much time on the Bill and is not moving ahead. We have made arrangements to group Clauses, Mr. Speaker; we have presented reasoned amendments; we have presented matters that have been brought to our attention by constituents who want answers from the Government; Member after Member has read into the record letters received from constituents, but the Government cannot tell them how to reply. In many cases the Minister cannot offer any help because even he cannot read the Bill.
The Minister and the Government want to eliminate democracy, to eliminate discussion and debate. They have some idea that they are the fount of all wisdom. From the Place Bell Canada tower in the City of Ottawa it seems they are going to try to control Canada, to control the business of Canada and, indeed, destroy the business of Canada.
The Minister mentioned that this Party toured Canada and held public hearings. In January, 1982, Mr. Speaker, 65 Members of this Party gave up part of their recess to hear public evidence on this issue and, as a result of that evidence, some changes were made. With other Members I came back to Ottawa in August and September to listen to witnesses give evidence on a Ways and Means motion. As a result of that evidence some other changes were made. There have also been other changes that deliberately went against the decision of the Finance Committee but the Government does not want to explain why it took this action.
There are matters in the Bill that still have to be dealt with, such as soft cost, RRSP interest deductibility, work in
progress, capital gains reserves, IAACs and so on. Representatives of the airlines have written to point out that the iniquitous tax imposed on Canadian airlines is responsible for some massive deficits.
The Government does not want to deal with the fact that the world price of petroleum has dropped dramatically but wants to ram through the provision of the Bill that deals with that matter. The Government does not believe that the people have the right to be heard. It believes that because it elected more Members to the House of Commons on February 18, 1980 than any other Party, it has the right to do what it damn well pleases. It believes that Members of Parliament are here for one purpose only, and that is to stand and bow to you, sir, when it decides to call a vote.
We have an obligation to represent our constituents and to represent all parts of the country, and some of them, Mr. Speaker, have no use for this Government. But they want to be represented and they demand to be represented.
The Government has brought in a motion for closure on this Bill. There is no justification for that, Mr. Speaker. It smacks of dictatorship and the House should not put up with it. There is a time when Governments have the right to move things along, when they can claim that there has been ample discussion, but that is not the case here. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) has a series of amendments to the Bill which he wants to present, but apparently he has now decided he does not care whether they are presented or not. All he wants to do is ram the Bill through, even though it contains errors in drafting and even though there are people like notaries who have not been covered in the exemption provisions. He does not care because his people in the Place Bell Canada tower know everything. They know how small business operates and how to crush it. They know how people want to protect their families with insurance and they know how to wreck that. They want to make sure that people do not save for their old age. They have an interest in grabbing as much money as they can.
The Government talks about fairness in the House, but when we point out that the provisions are not fair, it claims that it needs the money. In the last analysis it says: "If you do not pass the Bill we cannot pay the income tax rebates". Mr. Speaker, Section 152 of the Income Tax Act demands that the Government pay those rebates, so it is breaking the law if it does not. Anyone who has to borrow money because Government will not pay the rebate is borrowing because it has breached the Statutes of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to make a comment about the Government of Canada which, perhaps, is the lowest blow of all. The behaviour of the Liberal Government reminds me of the Social Credit Government of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER COMMITTEE STAGE OF BILL C-139
speechtext: That is the lowest blow!

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER COMMITTEE STAGE OF BILL C-139
speechtext:
The Government does not care about Parliament. It does not care that we are living in a participatory democracy; it just goes ahead with the actions it feels are in the best
March 15, 1983

interests of its Members and its friends as politicians, not of the people of Canada.
The Government of the Province of British Columbia thought it was going to be so short of money that it had to grab from the renters of British Columbia, so it arbitrarily changed the law. Without introducing a bill in the legislature it said that there was no longer an opportunity for people to claim the rental tax credit on this year's tax return. It informed the federal Government and, in the usual Liberal-Socred alliance, the Government agreed to co-operate.
That is the kind of mindless arrogance that has resulted in countless letters, telegrams, phone calls, night letters and briefs to Members of the Opposition Parties. People are saying that the tax Bill must be changed and that we must do what we can to stop this madness.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher) has said on a number of occasions, as has the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove), that because a certain number of days have been spent debating this Bill, it must pass. It is as if there is a secret formula whereby after so many days of debate a Bill must pass. It is as if it is not necessary to listen to the Opposition bringing forward their concerns and those of their constituents. It is as if the Government may just ignore reality, spend x number of days on the Bill and then it must pass.
I would remind the Minister of State for Finance that we have spent 12 days only at second reading and Committee stage considering 139 Clauses contained in 295 pages, designed to impose additional taxes at a time when the Canadian economy is on its knees. If those taxes could be considered fair and just and treated Canadians equally, I would co-operate fully with the Goverment. What we are dealing with is a tax Bill that is unfair, which treats one set of Canadians one way and another set of Canadians quite the contrary. It is a money grab of the most wicked kind. I will outline three of these four obvious concerns.
Let us consider first that last year thousands of Canadians who earned in excess of $50,000 did not pay one penny in income tax. Nothing has changed in this Bill to change that situation. As a matter of fact, the situation will be worse this year. The Bill before Parliament will have middle and low-income earners in Canada paying more taxes. Their taxes will be increased.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER COMMITTEE STAGE OF BILL C-139
speechtext: That is nothing new.

speechtext:
Upper income earners will have their taxes decreased. If you are making the taxable income in excess of $24,645, even the tax rate will be reduced three percentage points. In other words, the effective tax rate will be reduced from 28 per cent to 25 per cent if you have a tax rate in excess of $24,465.
However, if you are a real high income earner, earning in the area of $ 133,000, then your tax rate will be decreased from 43 per cent to 34 per cent. However, if you are a regular
Time Allocation
normal Canadian citizen, probably having your taxes deducted at source, you will maintain the same tax rate, but because of the deindexing proposition you will have increased taxes to pay. Liberals say that is fair, that it is in the best interests of all Canadians, Mr. Speaker.
We can look at another section. I hesitate to go into it because it becomes so incredibly obscene. It shows the difference between the taxes paid by individuals and the taxes paid by the corporate sector. I looked back to the year 1952. I found then that of all the federal tax revenues, 46 per cent were paid by individuals and 54 per cent were paid by corporations. In 1962 that situation changed. Of all federal tax revenues, 60 per cent came from individuals and 40 per cent came from the corporate sector. In 1980, of all federal tax revenues, 30 per cent came from corporations and 70 per cent came from individual taxpayers in Canada. Over the years, the situation has completely reversed. As the years go by more and more of the federal burden is being placed on the individual taxpayer while the corporate citizens pay less and less. As Members of the Government are bound to do, they rise in their seats and say, "But the corporate sector does pay income tax. It pays its fair share."
I want to identify two of our favourite corporate citizens, namely, the Royal Bank of Canada and the Bank of Montreal. Are people aware of how much these two corporate citizens, who did not do badly last year-the Royal Bank of Canada made $330 million before tax and the Bank of Montreal made $239 million before tax-paid in tax last year? How much income tax actually occurred in terms of their payment? These two corporate citizens paid no income tax, not a single penny. No income tax was paid, despite the hundreds of millions of dollars earned in profits. That is no fault of the Royal Bank of Canada or the Bank of Montreal. It is the fault of the Government of Canada which has allowed the banks to get away with this kind of financial skullduggery.
If you look at the big five banks in Canada-and last year was a difficult year for the banks-you will find they earned $1.6 billion. The five major banks paid in taxes a total of $132 million, or an effective tax rate of 8.1 per cent. That rate of 8.1 per cent is the tax rate of an individual who has a taxable income between $7,500 and $8,000 per year. I suspect that when you put the Royal Bank of Canada, the Bank of Montreal, and the other big banks alongside an individual whose taxable income is $7,500, there is something drastically wrong if they are sharing the same effective tax rate.
We see today a Bill which will influence the lives of every Canadian. We have seen the Government introduce a $6 billion blackmail charge against the Opposition by saying that we, in the Opposition, are holding $6 billion from going out to those people who ought to be receiving their tax refunds. That is absolutely not the case. If we had had a little co-operation from the Government benches and if the Government had shown us an indication that it was prepared to analyze seriously the tax Bill and to listen seriously to the concerns raised by

individuals and groups across the country, we would have been very co-operative. But there has not been a single example on the part of the Government to indicate its interest in approaching this situation in a co-operative way.

speechtext: I believe this is a very, very dark day for most Canadians when the Government, in which Canadians have put their faith over the last number of years and during one of the deepest depressions our country has experienced since 1930, is now going to impose 125 pages of new taxes on Canadians. If that is the Liberal's idea of assisting us during difficult times and if the Liberals are going to permit tax legislation to go through that still has such incredible injustices built into the system, we will continue to do everything we can to oppose this hideous piece of legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) should really stop misleading the Canadian people. I listened to him a few moments ago. There is just no truth in what he said. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South should at least get his facts straight. I can respect a difference of opinion, but I have no respect for a tactic which allows a man to stand in the House and give out information about tax returns which is blatantly false. It is shameful that he should have done that here this afternoon.
My good friend, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) needs a little friendly advice. He is the latest armchair socialist to take over the finance portfolio for the New Democratic Party. He has got it up here, Mr. Speaker, but he does not have it down here in the gut. He has no fire in the belly. He thinks socialism well but he does not act it well. He does not live it very well. But as a mental exercise, it is fascinating to listen to my good friend from Kamloops-Shuswap. Nevertheless, I will give him just a sentence of friendly advice. Before he gets to use particular examples about tax implications, he should really know what he is talking about. I say to him that before going public he should check his points because he will find he is wanting in some respects.
I listened with interest earlier to the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), who is out on the election circuit this afternoon, I would think, trying to get himself elected. It seems everyone on the other side these days is a leader looking for a Party. They are all looking for a Party. Among them is the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre who stood in his place and called for even more tax changes. He is not satisfied with the 125 pages, or whatever there are; he wants still more. I wish Hon.Members would get their heads together over there. Maybe they want 126 pages, maybe they want 124.5 pages. Could they make up their minds, Mr. Speaker? Could they all get together? I know they fight among themselves, but certainly on this important tax Bill they should be able to bury their hatchets and their knives and get their act together. They should decide whether they want more changes, fewer changes, the same number of changes on more pages or more changes on fewer pages. We are hearing it all,
Mr. Speaker. How does the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre square his call for more changes with his oft-repeated plea to end the uncertainty? Let us end the uncertainty, he says. Let us tell the taxpayers of Canada where we stand, he says in one mouthful, and in the next mouthful he says, "I have a few more changes I would like to have accommodated before we end the uncertainty."
Of course, he goes on to talk about how the Tories would reduce the deficit. Yet, while he makes those pledges, every additional tax change that he advocates would mean less Government revenue. How does he balance that with his call for decreasing the deficit? How can he decrease the deficit on one hand and advocate tax changes that would even further reduce the amounts accruing to the public Treasury on the other hand? How does he propose to reduce the deficit? He should be more specific on that particular point. Perhaps he will choose to be more specific about how he would reduce the deficit when he speaks during the leadership campaign.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

that the Member for Etobicoke Centre gave to the House, he said that Revenue Canada ought to go ahead and process the tax returns. On what assumptions? operating costs at an airport. It is totally unjustifiable. For days on end, the Liberals debate the cutting of 50 cents from the benefits of senior citizens and from Family Allowance or baby bonus cheques while they waste inexcusable amounts of money.

speechtext: We're bringing in closure because you are filibustering.

In one year, the Government wasted $1 billion propping up Petro-Canada and providing money to a Crown corporation, some $400 million being the cost of interest to the taxpayers of Canada, in order to keep it afloat. Over the past couple of days we have heard the nightmare story taking place in Montreal concerning Maislin Trucking. We have reason to be suspicious that the Government might continue with its policy of propping up a friend through the corporation known as Maislin Trucking.
We are also concerned about the expenses borne by commissions to determine, because the Government is incapable of determining it, why we are in such a heck of a mess in Canada. We are in such financial difficulty because the Government is incapable of dealing with the problem. Therefore, it also appoints failures from former Governments to sit on commissions at $800 a day to try to determine not only how we came to be in this mess, but also how we will get out of it. The reason they are out of it is because when they, as Ministers, were in it, they could not solve the problem themselves. That is the kind of waste of taxpayers' dollars about which we are concerned.
Further, we must sit here for an afternoon, realizing that at the end of the day's session the curtain has been brought down on discussions affecting industry, agriculture, and consumers in Canada. What about the payoffs in salaries and bonuses and the rip-offs involving former Cabinet Ministers, matters which we have been debating for some two months? Do the people of Canada realize that a former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, while he was in office, put himself in a position whereby he could influence existing Cabinet Ministers in order to turn a $25,000 investment into hundreds of thousands of dollars, if not close to three-quarters of a million dollars in taxpayers money, that giant rip-off being known as the "Coal-gate Affair"?
How much will the people take? How much does the Government expect them to take? How can the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) tell Members of the Official Opposition how the Liberals would reduce the deficit when they have been sitting there-

speechtext: Take you off the payroll.

speechtext:
-for the past two months, trying to justify those kind of horrendous nightmare stories? There is no excuse for it. We are dealing with an incapable Government. Hon. Members opposite take the opportunity to come into the House of Commons and spout off about what our Hon.
Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) says or what our Hon. Members from Toronto say, yet do not say anything specific.
I say, with all due respect, that the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's who just spoke in the House of Commons, made accusations against Members of the Official Opposition and spoke in innuendoes. Never once, in the preamble to his remarks on the Bill, did he give an example. He made the kind of statements which have caused the people of Canada to be concerned about the morality, integrity and honesty of Members of the Government, not only those on the front bench but also those on the backbenches.
I will close my remarks by saying that there is one area which simply cannot go without some comment. According to the current proposed legislation in the Bill, which is being subjected to closure, any change of ownership in life insurance policies would result in a disposition which would cause prebudget contracts to be deemed to be post-budget contracts. When have we heard that before from the Government? When, after a budget, has the Government stripped away contracts with civil servants which were signed prior to a budget? Through the six and five program, under the guise of bringing down inflation, it will take away 50 cents from a child allowance payment while we are spending $800 a day to feed a former Cabinet Minister's well-being.
Perhaps two situations merit exemptions from these rules, and we hope that in the third reading stage and in committee this will be accepted. First, under life insurance, I am referring to juvenile policies owned by a parent and, second, to policies owned by one spouse on the life of the other spouse. How can the Government justify its proposed changes which would remove those benefits and make them taxable?
In the second case, if, for example, a wife owned an insurance policy on the life of her husband but pre-deceased him, he could be expected to become the owner of the policy on his own life through the successor ownership clause. In this particular case again, an old pre-budget policy could become a post-budget policy and subject to new tax rules.
The Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's sits over there and asks why I read it. I read it because it is fact, and I want it recorded in Hansard. It is not fair. It is against all principles in the contracts signed in life insurance policies, which the Government is stripping away from the beneficiaries. Once again, the individual's efforts to become financially independent at the time of the death of a loved one or, in many cases, the passing on of a policy to a beneficiary, are thwarted by a Government. Some of these people have entered into contracts decades ago.
Also, the scheme for raising revenue becomes a source of immediate and ongoing liability. If a retiring policy holder does not have enough income, the Government will have to supplement it. Is it not better to let him use all policy funds in a life insurance policy before tax to buy the annuity and pay the tax on it?
March 15, 1983

Each crisis, be it the death of a parent or a spouse, the loss of a job, or old age, will result in further financial hardships as a result of the proposed changes to taxation of life insurance contracts. Does the Government really wish to make those already suffering suffer more?

Mr. Speaker, our purpose today is to consider the motion that was brought before the House with respect to the termination of the debate on Bill C-139 which amends the Income Tax Act of Canada. I do not know any piece of legislation on the statute books of the Parliament of Canada that affects more Canadians in a more important way than the income tax law. In the last reported taxation year, there were 15,100,000 Canadians who filed income tax returns, and of that number over 10 million paid income tax.
When we stand here in the House of Commons and look to our Leaders in the Government who tell us that we must end the debate on this taxation measure, I hope they realize that
they are talking to 15 million fellow Canadian citizens and 10 million taxpayers who might not want this debate ended, if they knew the manner in which they were affected by those tax measures.
We have heard speeches in this House of Commons made by Government Members that contain the worst kind of public deception. We just heard a speaker on the Government side talk about the months and months of delay in processing these tax measures. I have before me Bill C-139 which states on its front page, "First reading, December 7, 1982". One does not need a calendar to tell them that is a very few months ago. The Members on the Government side will say: "Yes, but the measures were there, they were there in another form and we had a chance to look at them in another form." Mr. Speaker, the form in which these tax measures came into the House of Commons was in the budget of the former Minister of Finance in November of 1981, and those tax measures were presented to the House of Commons at that time by the Minister of Finance who is no longer the Minister of Finance. Because of the stupidity and the gross deception of that November 1981 budget, he is no longer with us as Minister of Finance. He has gone off to destroy the rest of the world's economies, having destroyed the Canadian economy with his foolish, stupid and ill-conceived measures. It is those measures that are now presented to us in the form of Bill C-139.
Let me tell you something about those tax measures that were presented to the House of Commons by the Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen) when he was Minister of Finance for Canada. Those measures included a provision under which seven million working Canadians would have been taxed in respect of their health benefit plan. 1 am sorry that we in the Progressive Conservative Party stood in the House day after day after day and warned the Minister of Finance about the bad effects of that tax measure for all Canadians, because he withdrew that tax measure. If he had kept it in force, if he had taxed seven million working Canadians in respect of their health benefit plans, he would have been thrown out of office at the next election along with practically everyone on the other side of the House, because Canadians are not going to stand for the stupidity and the crass results of that kind of tax measure.
Over 45 of those original tax measures have been changed or abandoned or diluted in some other way. Unfortunately, one that was watered down when it should have been completely eliminated was the proposal of the then Minister of Finance in November of 1981 to remove from taxation exemption the $1,000 of pension income received by our senior citizens, if they were also involved in a Registered Retirement Pension Plan program.
What that meant was that thousands of members of the Canadian Armed Forces, of the municipal police forces and public servants across this land who retired early in their careers on small pensions and who had to provide for their later senior years when they could not work at all, were going to be deprived of that very small benefit that meant a great
March 15, 1983

deal to them. There again the former Minister of Finance, when he realized the effect of the tax measure, was shocked into action. He modified it. He did not withdraw it, which he should have done. He was afraid to admit to the people of Canada that he made such a terrible mistake. He listened to his advisers in the Department of Finance when they said this benefit ought to be taken away from our senior citizens, and thereby prevent them from providing for their later years in which they could not work or earn an income.
It is unfortunate for the Progressive Conservative Party politically that it prevented the Government from making these terrible mistakes because the Government and Government Members would have been punished in the polls at the next election. Instead, we stood here, as is our public duty, and performed our function as the representatives of the people and begged and cajoled the Government into making these changes. As a result, they will not suffer politically from the errors of the past. They had an opportunity to correct them.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) and other Members supporting the Government say in the House of Commons that we should allow these measures to pass immediately. It is unfortunate, as I said, that we did not allow them to pass originally because then they would have paid for their errors. As it is now, they managed to come out without those measures that will wreak havoc among Canadian taxpayers.
They still expect us to act on their advice, which is to pass their Bill. We cannot do that. We are the people who stand between the Government and the taxpayers of Canada. We are the ones who have to stop the Government of Canada when it brings forward tax measures that are harmful to the people of Canada. We have done that job, and we have done it well. We must continue to do it, we must continue to protect Canadians against their Government. That is the most unfortunate thing that I have ever said in this House of Commons, that we have to stand here and protect Canadian taxpayers, the citizens of Canada, against their Government, the Government that would have taxed their health benefit plan, that would have seen thousands of health benefit plans across Canada collapse because the workers were not willing to pay tax in respect of those benefits.
We had to stop that measure. We did stop the measure. What do those people on the other side of the House of Commons, the Members of the Liberal Party, condemn us for? They stand up and say we are delaying the refunds of taxes to the Canadian people; those Canadians who have overpaid their taxes will not get their refunds because of the delaying tactics. What kind of proposition is that for a responsible Member of Parliament, never mind a Cabinet minister, to take? He knows the reason why we are debating this Bill in the House of Commons. He knows the reasons why we have been all over the budget resolutions six ways to Sunday, studying them, trying to improve them.

The people of Canada know what we are doing in the House of Commons. The people of Canada know why they need all that revenue in the form of taxation. They need it to carry out their lustful expenditure programs. Canadian National Railways this year recorded a deficit of $220 million. That is after they sloughed off all their losing propositions such as VIA Rail and CN Marine. Air Canada has a deficit. The National Harbours Board had $400 million written off its past expenditures, $250 million for the Port of Montreal. The Petro-Canada budget is $2.7 billion, more than the whole of the Atlantic area. That Crown corporation is spending $2.7 billion. Do you think there is some waste there? They have 200 engineers with nothing to do. That is only the beginning. I could go on and on. Mirabel, $50 million a year, Dome Petroleum, Davie Shipbuilding $200 million on the Gulf Span Ferry which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) said would never be built.
Thank you for your indulgence, Mr. Speaker. I have at least another $2 billions' worth. I beg the chance to respond to the Member from Newfoundland.

It is evident that this Government does not know what it is doing when you consider that this is by far the longest session on record. We are getting very close now to three years of being in one session. Presumably, under normal conditions we would expect to have a Throne Speech and a budget debate and disposition of the Estimates on an annual basis, and that would be considered as one session of Parliament.
One cannot help but wonder why we have not encountered more of these problems sooner as far as this Government is
Time Allocation
concerned because effectively, as the Hon. Member who spoke previously pointed out, we are dealing with several budgets. We are dealing with the budget which came down in October of 1981 which was amended in April of 1982. We had what amounted to a mini-budget in June of 1982, and we had a financial statement or financial update from the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) last fall when we came back after the summer break. When you jam all of those things into one extremely large and complex Bill, it must amount to many technical amendments to the Income Tax Act. It is no wonder that the Government is pressed for time. For those of us in the Opposition who have concerns about some of the measures in the Bill which are going to affect our constituents adversely, it would be irresponsible of us to pass this Bill without having some kind of adequate discussion in the House. That is one of the issues which has to be addressed when we talk about closure.
I am a relatively new Member in the House, but I know this is the fourth time that we have had closure since this House returned on January 17. That clearly is an indication that the Government is not able to manage House time. 1 can give you an indication of where they could have saved one day's time. I am part of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedures, and one of the recommendations of the Committee was that the size of committees should be smaller. We recommended that the size of Committees move down from 20 to 30 Members to a range of 10 to 15 Members. There is a problem in terms of redistributing or allocating the memberships on the various committees so that it is in accordance, on a percentage basis, with the number of Members which each Party has in the House. What would be fair, I believe, as far as the smaller committees are concerned, is a figure of 11 Members. That would allocate six Members to the Government, four to the Official Opposition and one to the NDP. That would have been acceptable to our House Leader, and I think we would have been able to live with that. Instead, the Government chose to pick a figure of ten Members and divide it up so there were six Liberals, three Conservatives and one NDP. The reason the Government did that, we are told, is that the chairmen of the committees would be neutral and never have to vote. If you take the neutral chairmen, that leaves five Government Members to four Opposition Members. To my mind that is totally ludicrous. Under Standing Order 13, Mr. Speaker, you do not vote except in the case of a tie where the Speaker casts the tie-breaking vote. I do not know whether there has been a situation in this House where the Speaker has had to vote, but the provision is there in case of a tie.

Looking at it now, that rate cost the Canadian taxpayer something like $2 billion, a horrendous amount of money. We have suggested to the Government that it could have a better system of deciding on the appropriate rate for Canada Savings Bonds. Now, the $2 billion is an estimate, but it is a visible estimate. Surely we can devise something which is a lot simpler than the present form. Not only would it be simpler to fill out,
it would cost less to administer. Now, there are some suggestions which will not cost the Government any money. Presumably they could even save money by reducing the number of bureaucrats required. So we do make some sensible and worthwhile suggestions on this side of the House. I would point out that I get a little upset when I hear people on the other side stand up and not defend their own Government's program- which presumably they should be doing as part of the Government-but try to turn it around and say that all the Opposition does is to criticize. In the brief time I have had I have made two or three points which the Government could consider, so let them not accuse us of speaking out of both sides of our mouth. Too often we hear people say that the only time we suggest something is when it will increase the deficit. That is not the case in these suggestions I have made.
Let me close, Mr. Speaker, by making one final suggestion. I understand from the questions and answers during the Question Period today that there is a possibility that Maislin Transport might be losing something like $1 million a month. If that is the case and the Government is involved, I would suggest that the money could be much better used to bring down interest rates on farm improvement loans where farmers are locked in at 16.75 per cent, because from the figures I have seen that would be much more useful to the economy than simply pouring $1 million down the hole every month for a money losing trucking outfit.

This debate started on November 12, 1981. There was a full budget debate. Then we had announcements from the Minister of Finance on December 18. I was in the House then so I know there were extended questions at that time. Then there was another budget brought in on June 28, 1982. There was a big, long discussion then. For a few Members of Parliament who chose to take advantage of it, the committee sat through the months of August and September and had carried on detailed discussions. Then we had a financial statement on October 27.
Then this Bill was brought in. On this Bill alone, Mr. Speaker, we have had seven days' debate on second reading, and so far more than four days' debate in Committee of the Whole. We have had over 75 Tory speakers participating on second reading, and 18 NDP Members, more than half their caucus in each case, Mr. Speaker. And what do we hear today? "We have not had a chance to say enough". Well, Mr. Speaker, if they have not had enough time after two budget debates, a financial statement, a special debate in the House and 11 days in Parliament then you are windbags and you do not deserve any more time.
Let us look at some of what we have accomplished, Mr. Speaker, because, quite frankly, this discussion really was fruitful and we should be honest about that. Some of the Members on the other side made contributions, just as did Members on our side.
March 15, 1983

From last April until February of this year there was extended debate with associations and business groups in the country about the federal sales tax. A budget paper was prepared and published. The business groups advised the Government, and the result was a new process for analysing a special new tax. The same thing happened with the Lortie Commission. We also have a new set of rules for charities. When the Finance Committee studies tax measures, new ground was broken.
A new technique of pre-budget consultation was practised by the former Minister of Finance last spring, and has been carried on by the present Minister through December and January. People from outside Government have been giving advice. A whole new set of rules on interest expense deductions has been drawn up and has been examined by them. Health and dental plans have been debated and, on the advice of outsiders, those provisions were dropped from the Bill. The advice the Government received from outside has been invaluable. Changes were made to the provisions governing work in progress, soft costs for construction and insurance regulations after over a year of negotiation with the industry, and there has been a change in the automobile standby charge provision. Anyone who claims that the Bill has not had adequate debate is debasing the advice received from outside groups who have made a real contribution to the process.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad of the opportunity to speak against the Government's decision to choke off debate on this Bill. The Hon. Member who just spoke bragged about the months that have been spent in delaying the Bill. It is 13 months since the 1981 budget, and during that time the Government carried on discussions with those people it wished to consult and suffocated public debate on the Bill. When it did introduce the Bill it made sure it was debated a day here and a day there, often on short notice. This was to make it as difficult as possible for the Opposition to comment wisely. The Government even played games with the use of time allocation in order to make things more difficult for the Opposition.
I have spoken on many occasions about one of the most unjust clauses in the Bill. Clause 64 removes the exemption for immigrants who send money to relatives overseas, except for a spouse, child or grandchild. I hope Hon. Members will vote against this Clause. Most immigrants earn low incomes. Although the Government says that some immigrants were claiming exemptions to which they were not entitled, the total amount of money that it would have been impossible for them to take improperly would be far less than one major corporation, such as Shell, could take by means of the loopholes provided by the Government. It is unjust for the Government to crack down on immigrants when it does not crack down on the 4,000 individuals who earn over $100,000 but pay no tax whatsoever. The Government does not crack down on Shell Oil which sometimes pays no tax whatever on a quarter of a billion dollars. Those immigrants are not among those who had an opportunity to be consulted in the consultation process bragged about by the Parliamentary Secretary. They were excluded from consultation by the simple process of not publicizing the occasions.
Another interesting fact that has not been brought out concerns the injustice of the present tax system. In no way has it been addressed by all the consultations and private discussions this Government has had with wealthy corporations and with the promoters of wealthy corporations. Government officials have not talked with working people nor have they talked to representatives of the garment industry. I mention this because Spadina is one of the areas in Canada where the garment industry is important. It employs about 10,000 people in Spadina. The garment industry has been compelled to subsidize industries like the oil industry, the banking industry and the mining industry. From 1976 to 1979 the taxation rate on the garment industry, clothing and textiles, was about 87 per cent higher than the average taxation rate on the oil, the mining and the banking industries. In fact, if the oil, the mining and the banking industries had been effectively taxed at the same rate as the textile and garment industry, this Government would have $1.7 billion more in its coffers and it would have no excuse for the cutbacks it has made in health, education and social housing. Instead, this Government preferred to give the tax break, not to an industry where wages are low and modernization is urgently needed, but to an industry that has more money than it knows what to do with
and exports money out of Canada. Another way of putting the point is that in Government benefits to industry, the garment and textile industry has had about $27 per employee per year, according to a 1978 Government study. Compare this $27 per employee per year in the garment industry with an average of $179 for industry as a whole. We know which industries pull that average up. Again it is the oil, the banking and the mining industries. Not only does the Government not take tax at the same rate from those wealthy industries but it gives assistance to the already wealthy industries at a rate several times higher than the rate at which it assists the garment industry.
I want to point out some of the long-standing injustices that have been noted, but noting them has made no difference to the Government's interest in correcting them. It has been pointed out that the statutory rate of taxation that is imposed on corporations generally is more than 46 per cent. In 1978, what corporations actually paid was around 30 per cent. Already a deception has occurred because the average taxpayer is not able to cut his personal tax bill by two-thirds as corporations have generally done. Again, the smaller corporations in the more hard pressed industries get less of this tax break than the richer ones.
Consider some of the tax rates paid. Cadillac-Fairview, according to a Government study, has been making $100 per month surplus on every one of its 15,000 apartments in Toronto. Every one of those 15,000 units nets Cadillac-Fairview on average $100 a month surplus. What sort of taxation does Cadillac-Fairview pay? The rate is 6 per cent. The Steel Company of Canada pays 7 per cent. Big deal! Union Gas pays a little under 6 per cent. The Toronto Dominion Bank, my goodness, it paid 18 per cent one year. Let us take a look at what happens to ordinary people and immigrants. Immigrants try to send money to relatives overseas, a family obligation which they recognize. This is a family obligation we value and claim to respect in this country. But those working people who are trying to send money to relatives overseas are generally taxed at a far higher rate than are corporations. If we pass this Government Bill, through Section 64 we will penalize people for acknowledging and acting on family obligations.
We are continuing to allow massive multi-billion dollar gifts to the wealthiest people, either individuals or corporations in this country, while we chisel working people who may earn $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 a year in order to support their families. We chisel them by whittling money off and causing the lowest income people of this country to pay a far higher proportion of their earnings in tax than is paid by the people earning the highest incomes.
This whole tax Bill which the Government has put forth is a disgrace. When we come to Section 64 I would ask that Members of this House have the decency to vote against it.

Mir. Louis Duclos (Montmorency-Orleans): Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to take a few minutes to tell the House why I believe that the Government is quite justified in putting an end
March 15, 1983

to this debate. I shall not deal with the substance of this bill. During the last few months, the Opposition parties have had ample time to explain why they believe that some of the provisions of this bill should be amended. They may be right in certain cases, but obviously, they may also be wrong.
However, I would like to appeal to the sense of responsibility of the Opposition Members and ask them to show more understanding of the role of Parliament in a democratic society such as ours. Once members of a party have been elected democratically and allowed to air their views on behalf of the interests they represent, 1 do not think that they are entitled to obstruct systematically the operation of our democratic institutions.
Mr. Speaker, I find this bill satisfactory. It might not be perfect, but I believe that it is a good bill because it is prompted by a desire to be fair to Canadian taxpayers as a whole. I am well aware that most of the spokesmen for the Official Opposition have risen on behalf of special, not to say privileged, groups in our society, who are literally haunted by the prospect of having to share some of their wealth with the most disadvantaged members of our society, while the members of the leftist party have made speeches aimed mostly at placing an even heavier fiscal burden on the shoulders of the private sector, which remains the motor of development, progress and economic growth in a society such as ours.
Mr. Speaker, I would like the Opposition Members to show at least some sense of their responsibilities and remember that, by delaying this bill, they are penalizing underprivileged people in our society. For instance, they are penalizing those who, after working a few months early in 1982, now receive unemployment insurance and expect a rather substantial income tax refund. As long as this bill has not been passed by Parliament, the Department of National Revenue does not have the right or the authority to mail out the tax refunds to these people who are impatiently waiting for amounts which can be rather substantial. The Members opposite should also think about low income mothers who are waiting for this bill to be passed to receive their child tax credit, which can amount to over $1,000 in the case of a family with three children. These people are penalized by the filibustering which we have been witnessing in this House for too many weeks already.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) said earlier that, since the budget was brought down in November 1981, Opposition Members have had a total of 25 days of debate in this House to express their views. Moreover, in many cases, we have accepted suggestions by the Opposition as well as by Government Members. First, there was the debate on the budget of November 1981; then, there was another debate on the budget of June 1982; later on, in September 1982, the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs spent about a month examining all amendments to the Income Tax Act resulting from these two budgets. These amendments were examined one at a time and recom-
Time Allocation
mendations made to the Minister of Finance who accepted many.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there has of course been the present debate during which, as mentioned by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher), 75 Members of the Official Opposition, or about three quarters of them, have had the opportunity to voice their concerns or points of disagreement about this legislation. I also believe that nearly 20 Members of the New Democratic Party have risen during this debate to express their views about this Bill.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Government is acting responsibly, or perhaps that we are trying to make up for the lack of responsibility which seems to exist on the other side of the House, in deciding that what is at stake is so important that we must act now so that Canadians who are waiting for and are entitled to government refunds can receive them.

Mr. Speaker, in the remaining time that I have I would like to point out once again, for the record, the annoyance that we on this side feel at the Government's having introduced this motion under Standing Order 82 to terminate debate on this very important measure during the Committee of the Whole stage of Bill C-139. If one listens to the intensity of the speeches made earlier by the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) and the Member who just resumed his seat, I think it is obvious to Members on this side that the Government Members feel very uncomfortable about many of the initiatives which remain in this mammoth Bill C-139 which is some 295 pages and contains 134 separate Clauses dealing with matters of tax reform that affect virtually every Canadian citizen in several ways.
The anxiety felt by Members opposite stems from that day back on November 12, 1981, when the former Minister of Finance introduced his first budget. It was the basis for these reforms which the Government is now trying to implement retroactively. Even after it has been collecting taxes for over a year based on certain of these initiatives, it is trying to create a mood of desperation in the country. The Government is suggesting that it is the Opposition who is holding up these very important tax reforms. In fact, those of us who have travelled the country and have listened to our constituents know that there are still many serious and fundamental flaws with this legislation that will haunt Canadians and hinder the development of our economy for many years to come.
It strikes us as being strange that in this session, which is the longest in Canadian parliamentary history, the government has had to use time allocation and closure 20 times, beginning with the famous Friday in October of 1980 when closure was used to limit and suppress the rights of Opposition Members to debate the resolution on the Constitution of Canada that was introduced in the House. The outrage that Members of Parlia-

March 15, 1983
Time Allocation
ment and Canadians from every part of this land felt as a consequence of that initiative still prevails in this country today, as any poll would quickly reveal to Government Members. That outrage arose not only because closure was used in a most inappropriate way on that occasion when we all wanted to have a say on the future Constitution of this nation, but because closure was used on several subsequent important occasions.
There was an attempt by the Government to try to frustrate the right of Canadian citizens to watch the committee hearings on the Canadian Constitution during the winter of 1981. Closure was brought in on other important measures, such as the reform of the Canada Lands Act, Bill C-48.
In the spring of 1981 we saw closure used to limit debate on the final disposition of the Constitutional resolution. Had it not been for a stand-off in the House, we might well have had an entirely different Constitution enacted from the one we have today. It was only because of the resistance shown by Members on this side at that time that some very serious and divisive measures were not imposed upon Canadians by the will of the Liberal majority opposite.
I,	and I know the majority of Canadians, will consent to the attempt by the Opposition in the House to ensure that the Government does not hastily pass some 134 separate items of tax reforms through the House, in a Bill which is 295 pages thick, with only four days' debate at committee stage and only seven days' debate at second reading stage. There are items in this legislation which cover all sectors of the Canadian economy and affect farmers, the forest industry, the manufacturing industry, small-businessmen, fishermen, those who are employed in trade unions and those who are employed in the north.

speechtext:
1.	For the fiscal year (a) 1980-81 (b) 1981-82 (c) 1982-83 (d) 1983-84 (e) 1984-85, did the Government commit itself to provide assistance to foreign countries, through either Petro-Canada International or CIDA, to aid in the exploration for and development of potential oil and gas reserves and, if so, for each country, what amount of aid was committed?
2.	What increases in proven reserves, if any, have been achieved so far?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: AID TO COUNTRIES FOR OIL AND GAS EXPLORATION
speechtext:
I am informed by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Canadian International Development Agency as follows: In so far as Petro-Canada International Assistance Corporation is concerned:
1.	(a)-(e) Petro-Canada International became operational in January, 1982 and has committed assistance for preexploration and exploration activities to the following three countries: Jamaica-commitments of $6.8 million for 1982 and 1983; Tanzania-commitments of $29.4 million for 1982 and 1983; Senegal-commitments of $16.2 million for 1982, 1983 and 1984.
2.	No increases in proven reserves has been achieved so far. Exploration activities are only in the preliminary stage at this time.
3.	Not applicable.
In so far as the Canadian International Development Agency is concerned:
Pakistan
1.	Since 1973, Canada has financially supported the Oil and Gas Development Corporation in Pakistan by approximately $31 million committed to date for the Corporation's activities in drilling, production and technical assistance in the oil and gas sector. At the present time the Government of Canada anticipates possible cash disbursements during the next two fiscal years of most of the balance of the line of credit.
2.	There is no reliable information on the increases in proven reserves since the Government of Pakistan and the World Bank data are different. The seismic equipment in use has identified typical structures but volume estimates of the reserve are not possible to determine. However, because of the joint efforts of the three principal donors, the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and CIDA, significant discoveries have resulted over the last six years.
3.	In the case of oil, prospects are mixed for increasing production from existing oil fields in Pakistan. The Fifth Five-Year Plan called for production to increase from .49 million tons per annum in fiscal year 1978 to 1.7 million tons per annum in Fiscal year 1983 (10,000 barrels per day to 35,000 barrels per day). In fact, as a result of overly optimistic estimates of production per well, pricing problems, drilling problems and management problems, production remained virtually constant at 10,000 barrels per day until 1980-81,

March 15, 1983
Order Paper Questions
improving in 1982 mainly as a result of increased production from the Toot oil field and new production at 2,200 barrels per day from the Khaskeli oil field.
Production from Khaskeli could increase to some 5,000 barrels per day and production from the Meyal field is expected to increase to 13,000 barrels per day by 1987. If these targets are met, total production from known fields could reach 20,000 barrels per day by 1990.
The Directorate General, Energy and Resources, is projecting 20,000 barrels per day by 1985-86 and 27,000 barrels per day by 1989-90. In light of the recent World Bank unofficial reserves estimates such production figures are unlikely to be met unless upcoming tests on Toot and Dhodak prove to be very positive. Even with positive results on the assessment of these known fields it is likely that one additional field of Meyal proportions would have to be found and developed before 1990 to ensure that the 27,000 barrels per day figure is met for that year.
India
1.	In the case of CID A, two lines of credit have been extended to India:
A loan agreement for up to $15 million line of credit was signed on June 24, 1980 with the objective of increasing the proportion of Indian self-sufficiency in petroleum by contributing to the exploration and development of Indian oil and gas reserves. This line of credit was virtually fully committed by October 31, 1982. A second line of credit for up to $45 million was signed on November 21, 1981 with the same objectives. It is expected to be fully committed by November of 1984.
Disbursements under the $15 million line of credit should be completed by March of 1983. Disbursements under the $45 million line of credit are expected to be completed by fiscal year 1987-88.
2.	Accurate information on the increases in proven reserves is virtually impossible to determine since the Oil and Natural Gas Committee's (ONGC) program spans both offshore and onshore sites all over India. Announcements are made on a regular basis of the Government of India's intention to undertake major new drilling contracts and the ONGC has recently announced its intention to buy or lease a large number of new rigs in the next year or two. The line of credit, however, is designed in part to develop markets for Canadian industries and has, as such, no direct impact on the identification and exploration of oil and gas reserves.
3.	India's precarious energy situation is such that every discovery is being exploited as quickly as possible to reduce the costly import of oil. The Government of India has identified oil exploration and development as an essential component in meeting many of the other objectives in their Sixth Five-Year Plan. Shortages of oil impact in the power sector, in manufacturing, etc. to such a large extent that commercial development of new reserves is proceeding with all possible speed.

speechtext: Pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 58, I do now leave the chair for the House to go into Committee of the Whole.

On Clauses 8, 9 and 128(12)-

Mr. Chairman, when we rose earlier, I was asking the Minister about the Income Tax Act, Section 15.1, Subsection 11, which is Subclause 8(6). The penalty section has been changed. It originally stated that a penalty is imposed where a false declaration is made in a joint election in respect of a qualifying debt obligation. I am wondering if the Minister would explain to the House what the original problems were, their extent, and what is being corrected with this new provision?

Mr. Chairman, the difficulty in responding immediately in detail to the question is, of course, that the administration of the Act is under another Ministry, that of Revenue Canada. I can indicate that my officials point out that it was because of some experience with fraudulent declarations under the section that the amendment was brought forward. I do not have at my Fingertips the experience of the Revenue Department, but it is something I can obtain for the Hon. Member, and I will provide those details once I have had an opportunity to consult with the officials from the other Ministry.

Mr. Chairman, would the Minister make that undertaking to the House? It is rather important to us to know whether the fraudulent acts were the acts of individuals or through lending institutions. Does the Minister have any general information on that point?

Mr. Chairman, again because it involves another Ministry, I do not have the particulars. I hasten to assure the Hon. Member that when I have those particulars I will undertake to provide them on the next occasion we consider this matter in Committee of the Whole. My officials have brought to my attention that it would be a fairly recent experience inasmuch as the original Section was introduced in the 1979 Income Tax Act. I am referring to Section 15.1(6) under the heading "False Declaration". This is now expanded

March 15, 1983
Income Tax
to include not only corporations but individuals. So there may not be a lot of expenrience but I will attempt to get the information and I do not undertake to make it available to all Hon. Members who are interested in these proceedings.

Mr. Chairman, I would like the Minister to consider Clause 9 which relates to Section 15.2 of the Income Tax Act. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that the explanatory notes to the Bill are tremendously beneficial to those of us who are not skilled in reading those very complicated Sections. This is a very valuable addition in trying to figure out exactly where these Clauses are and what they really mean. In the explanatory notes, referring to Clause 9(a), it says the issuer cannot deduct the interest on the bond but the recipient of the interest is deemed to have received a taxable dividend from a taxable Canadian corporation. That raises the question, Mr. Chairman, as to what has been the cost to the Consolidated Revenue Fund of the bonds issued to date and what is the anticipated loss in the future.

Mr. Chairman, my officials are attempting to find that figure. I might say that I am very pleased some Members have found the innovation of explanatory notes useful because some other Members of this House have been very unkind to the Government in this respect and used it as an example of yet another complication and more paper work required by Government. I am very pleased some Members have found it useful because that was the intent of providing the explanatory notes. I know some members of the public have indicated it has been helpful.
On an annual basis the projection of the amendments which are before us would be that the cost to the CRF would be $25 million. Under the Section as it stood previously, that is the expansionary interpretation for use of the bond, the cost thus far, which is a bit harder, is calculated to be $125 million.

Mr. Speaker, the same Clause states that the bond must be issued after November 12, 1981, and before 1984. Does the Minister anticipate this provision going beyond 1984? As he well knows, we are almost into 1984 now, and he has actual experience to this point. Why would the Minister not consider an amendment which would take it, say, to 1985, which would then give people still more certainty as to whether or not they can get a bond?

Mr. Chairman, I indicated this morning in response to another line of questioning, I think it was from the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, that, number one, we have targeted the aid under the amendments toward, for example, people in very difficult circumstances who will use the bond where otherwise they might go into bankruptcy. subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-RESPONSIBILITY FOR ACTIONS BY MINISTERS AND OFFICIALS. (B) GOVERNMENT MANDATE
THE ADMINISTRATION-RESPONSIBILITY FOR ACTIONS BY MINISTERS AND OFFICIALS. (B) GOVERNMENT MANDATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for many years Canadians have been concerned about the changing standard of morality under the Government of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). There was a time, for example, when election promises were related to the Government's legislative program, but that is no longer the case. For many months, even years, Canadians have been trying to decipher the standard of morality of the Government. It has been coming to light in bits and pieces but has become more clear in what we now know as the "Gillespie affair". That is why on March 2 I put the following question to the Prime Minister:
On February 17, in answer to a question from the Hon. Member for Provench-er, the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 22938 of Hansard:
Yes, Madam Speaker, we are collectively responsible for the policies of this Government-
The Government as a whole is not collectively responsible for some individual agreement-
That is the nub of the problem in the country, Mr. Speaker. The Government wants to be accountable for concepts but not for administration. Putting it another way, the Government wants to be accountable for discussing an issue but not to be responsible when it makes a blatant error, as was the case in the Gillespie affair. That is why the Prime Minister replied to my question as reported at p. 23366 of Hansard as follows:
If the Hon. Member is talking about the meaning of responsible Government, literally, it means that the Government of the day is responsible to Parliament and can only continue exercising its powers with the authority of Parliament, that is, with the support of the majority of the Members of Parliament. That is what responsible Government means.
March 15, 1983

I think you will agree that that is a new definition of responsible Government.
We are now faced with a choice between the old concept of honour and the new concept of legality. The Prime Minister now seems to be defining responsible Government in terms of legality-if it is within the law, then it is all right. For many centuries women were not legally protected against wife beating but, just because there was no law prohibiting wife beating, that did not make it morally right to do so. It would appear that with the new standards of morality recognized by the Government, there will have to be a limitless agenda of laws to define what the Government can or cannot do. I do not dispute the fact that the law is an important protection, but if the law is the only protection, then conviction of an offence is the only way we can make the Government accountable.
The second part of the Prime Minister's definition is that if Parliament or a majority of Government Members validate any wrongdoing, that constitutes responsible Government. That raises all kinds of possibilities. If the Government can pistolwhip its backbenchers into voting for anything it says, then that will validate anything it does. That, by the Prime Minister's definition, is responsible Government.
I say again, and the Hon. Member can talk any time he wants to, that leaves out any kind of place for honour. It seems to me that we can trust anyone who knows nothing about law as long as they know a lot about honour. But you cannot trust someone who knows all about law but has no sense of honour. That is the choice we have in this country.
This Prime Minister is misdirecting and redirecting the cause of the whole Parliamentary system by redefining responsible Government to mean anything the Government will validate by a majority of Members-meaning if Government Members fall into line with anything the Prime Minister says-is responsible Government.
It was old Falstaff, the drunkard in the battle described by Shakespeare in Henry IV Part I who said, "What is honour? It is a mere scutcheon." It is kind of a coat of arms that you can toss aside. You can change loyalty, depending upon who your leader is because all you do is follow the standard. What did Falstaff do? He ran away in the heat of battle. He became a deserter because honour meant nothing. That becomes the shifting sand of the kind of morality which the Prime Minister is introducing. It means that morality is relative. There is no fixed standard and the Government can get away with anything as long as all of its lackies do anything it wants them to do.
